_notes: Group-generated events for the parochial vicar years (DESIGN.md 10). Every event carries a top-level group condition so @group_leader binds to a matching group of the current parish; type-gated events rebind the same group on a later fire because the generator gives a parish at most one group of each type. Events gated only on hostile:false bind to any non-hostile group and serve as the general parish texture (hall, bulletin, chaplain, money, Holy Week). Threads opened and resolved in this file: pv_grp_chaperone (pv_grp_youth_chaperone -> pv_grp_youth_chaperone_returns), pv_grp_empire (pv_grp_empire_beloved -> pv_grp_empire_reckoning). Flags defined here: pv_grp_chaperone_cleared / pv_grp_chaperone_ignored (how the uncleared chaperone was handled; read by the thread resolver), pv_grp_empire_confronted / pv_grp_empire_documented / pv_grp_empire_ignored (how the empire-builder was first handled; documented unlocks the graceful exit), pv_grp_svdp_quiet (the family was placed through another parish), pv_grp_tlm_learned (the player learned the older form; raises the chancery-call weight), pv_grp_recovery_attends (a player with past:drinking began attending closed meetings), pv_grp_ya_evening_mass (added a standing Sunday evening Mass), pv_grp_founded_handed_over / pv_grp_founded_legacy (a founded group was handed to its leader / outgrew the player), pv_grp_chaplain (the player holds a group chaplaincy; gates pv_grp_chaplain_ask off and is the hook for a future weekly AP commitment, which events cannot yet create). Risks recorded: pv_grp_chaperone_lapse, pv_grp_svdp_loan, pv_grp_bible_drift, pv_grp_rcia_reception. No flag here is read outside this file.

events.title: The Second Van
events.body: The youth retreat is in eleven days and {@group_leader} has the vans, the deposit, the permission slips, and a problem she raises with you in the parking lot rather than the office. One of the chaperones for the second van is a father who has driven for the group for years. His safe environment clearance lapsed in the spring. The renewal takes a background check and a training session, and the next session the diocese offers is the week after the retreat. She has already asked everyone else. Without him the second van does not go, and the second van is the sophomores. She says this the way people say things when they have decided and want you to agree. He is a good man. Everyone knows him. The policy exists precisely for the people everyone knows, which is the sentence you do not say in a parking lot. {@dre} keeps the compliance binder and will notice, or will not, depending on whether anyone shows her the roster. You are the priest the kids like. You are also the priest whose name is on the trip form.
events.flavorPrompt: A parking-lot conversation with a competent volunteer who has already decided. No villains. The rule is dull and correct and everyone in the scene knows it.

choices.label: No clearance, no van. Tell her tonight and help her find someone
choices.outcome: She is angry in the way of someone who has done all the work and been told it is not enough. You spend two evenings on the phone and find a mother who was cleared for the school. The second van goes. {@group_leader} does not thank you, and the father hears from someone that you were the reason, which is true.

choices.label: It is eleven days and he is a known man. Let it go this once
choices.outcome: You say nothing to {@dre} and she does not ask. The roster goes in the binder with his name on it and a clearance date nobody checks. {@group_leader} squeezes your arm. You have made a friend and a precedent, and you know which one lasts longer.

effects.value: Signed off a youth trip with an uncleared chaperone

choices.label: Put it on {@pastor}'s desk. It is his parish
choices.outcome: {@pastor} reads the roster, looks at you over it, and asks why you are bringing him a decision the policy has already made. He makes the call himself and the father stays home. {@group_leader} blames you anyway, because you were the one who could have fixed it and chose not to try.

choices.label: Drive the second van yourself
choices.outcome: You are cleared, you are ordained, and you are free that weekend if you make yourself free. {@group_leader} is delighted. {@pastor} covers the Saturday vigil and says nothing pleasant about it. You spend three days with fourteen sophomores and come back hoarse, behind on everything, and remembered.

events.title: The Audit Letter
events.body: The diocesan safe environment office does a rolling audit, and this year the roll lands on {parish}. The letter asks for the rosters of every youth event in the last twelve months with clearance dates beside each adult name. {@dre} brings it to you rather than to {@pastor}, which tells you she knows something or suspects it. She has the binder open on your desk to the retreat page. If the second van's driver was replaced, the page says so and the audit is a morning's work. If he was not, the page is a lie in your handwriting, and the office will find it, because finding it is what the office is for. {@group_leader} calls while {@dre} is still in the room. She has heard about the letter from the parish secretary and wants to know what you are going to tell them. The kids are back at school. The retreat was, by every account, the best in years.
events.flavorPrompt: An audit letter, a binder, and two women waiting in different rooms for the same answer. Administrative dread, not melodrama.

choices.label: Hand over the binder. The roster is clean
choices.outcome: The audit takes a morning. The office sends a form letter thanking {parish} for its compliance, and {@dre} pins it to the corkboard where {@group_leader} will see it. Nobody mentions the second van again, which is the reward for having done it right: nothing happens, and nothing continues to happen.

choices.label: Call the office yourself before they find it
choices.outcome: You tell the safe environment coordinator exactly what happened and that the decision was yours. She is quiet, then brisk: a letter in your file, a mandatory refresher, the father barred from driving until cleared. {@pastor} is told. {@group_leader} is furious that you told, then, a month later, less so. The kids never know.

effects.key: Self-reported a safe environment lapse on a youth trip

choices.label: Have the driver's renewal backdated by the training office's friend of a friend
choices.outcome: {@group_leader} knows someone. The renewal appears in the system dated the week before the retreat, and the binder page is true after the fact. The audit passes. You have now asked a layperson to falsify a diocesan record on your behalf, and she knows you did, and you know she knows.

effects.value: A backdated safe environment clearance for a youth trip

choices.label: Tell {@dre} the truth and let her decide what the binder says
choices.outcome: {@dre} listens, closes the binder, and says she will handle the audit. You do not ask how. The audit passes. She has done you a favor she did not want to do, and the debt is hers to collect. {@group_leader} hears that {@dre} covered for the group and softens toward her, which is the one good thing.

effects.value: A staff member covered a safe environment lapse for you

events.title: The Lock-In
events.body: The youth group's lock-in is Friday: forty teenagers in the hall from eight until seven, pizza, a movie the parents were told is rated PG, a scavenger hunt through the church with the lights off, and Mass at midnight if a priest will say it. {@group_leader} would like the priest to be you, and would like you to stay for the part after Mass when the kids are tired enough to talk. {@pastor} used to do it and stopped. You are twenty years younger than he is and it shows in what people ask of you. The Saturday after a lock-in is a Saturday you do not get back: confessions at three, the vigil at five, and a homily you had meant to finish Friday night. The kids will remember whether you were there. They will not remember the homily either way.
events.flavorPrompt: Cheerful, slightly exhausting. Teenagers as a real presence, not a sentiment.

choices.label: Say the midnight Mass, then go to bed
choices.outcome: You say Mass in the dark church to forty kids in sweatshirts, which is more attention than you get on Sunday. You are in bed by one and functional by nine. {@group_leader} is grateful for what she got and does not say what she wanted.

choices.label: Stay the whole night
choices.outcome: You are there at three when a junior tells you her parents are separating and at five when two boys ask, seriously, about the seminary. Saturday is a ruin. The homily is last year's. {@group_leader} tells everyone you stayed, and the parents hear it, and the kids already knew.

choices.label: Decline. The pastor can bless them at the 9:00 on Sunday
choices.outcome: {@group_leader} finds a deacon from the next parish to lead a prayer service at midnight, and he does it well, and the kids are fine. She is not, quite. The group notices which priest shows up for the night that is theirs and which does not, and it is the kind of thing teenagers notice without saying and remember without meaning to.

events.title: The Banner
events.body: {@group_leader} has chartered a bus for the vigil outside the clinic on the state road, and has had a banner made: the parish's name in eighteen-inch letters over a line of Scripture. She wants you on the bus in a collar, and she wants to announce it from the pulpit, and she wants it in the bulletin with a photo afterward. {@pastor} has told her, for three years running, that the parish prays for the unborn in the intercessions and that is the parish's position. He has not told her no about the banner because she has not asked him; she is asking you. The clinic's neighbors have written to the paper before. The paper has printed the letters. A priest on that sidewalk is a photograph, and a photograph with the parish's name over his head is a position the whole parish has taken whether or not it was consulted. A priest who stays home is also a photograph, in the album the group keeps.
events.flavorPrompt: The banner as the real object: eighteen-inch letters, a parish name, a state road. Nobody in the scene is unserious.

choices.label: Go, in the collar, under the banner
choices.outcome: You stand on the sidewalk for three hours in the cold and pray the Rosary twice through. Someone photographs you. It runs in the paper with the parish's name legible. The group has never been so alive. Two families write to {@pastor} to say they will be looking for a different parish, and he forwards the letters to you without comment.

choices.label: Go, but no banner and no announcement. As a private citizen who happens to be a priest
choices.outcome: You are there in a coat, no collar, and you pray with them. The banner stays on the bus. {@group_leader} takes this as half a betrayal and half a victory and cannot decide which. Nobody photographs you. The group's numbers do not move, and neither does the paper.

choices.label: Stay home. Offer the Mass that morning for the intention and say so
choices.outcome: You announce at Mass that it is offered for the group's intention, and you mean it. It is not what she asked for. The bus leaves without you. {@group_leader} tells the group the parish's priests do not support them, which is unfair and partly true. The letter to the paper that week names no parish.

choices.label: Tell her a parish is not a lobby, and the banner is out of the question
choices.outcome: You say it to her, then to the group, because she asks you to. You say the parish prays and serves and does not picket under its own name. Someone records it. It circulates. The paper's letter this month praises {parish} for restraint, which is worse in some rooms than the banner would have been.

events.title: The Insert
events.body: The bulletin goes to the printer Thursday at noon and {@secretary} brings you the pro-life group's insert at eleven-forty because {@pastor} is at the deanery meeting and someone with a collar has to initial it. It is a full page. Half of it is the diaper drive, which is unobjectionable and useful. The other half is a paragraph about a bill in the legislature with the names of the representatives who voted for it and the word shameful used twice. {@group_leader} wrote it. She writes well. {@secretary} has the printer on hold and is watching the clock. You are aware that the bulletin is the most-read document the parish produces, that its contents are legally the parish's speech, and that a page like this has cost other parishes a phone call from the diocesan attorney about their tax status. You are also aware it is eleven-forty-three.
events.flavorPrompt: A clock, a printer on hold, a secretary who wants an initial. Small, fast, and consequential in a way nobody in the room will admit.

choices.label: Run the diaper drive. Cut the paragraph
choices.outcome: You initial the top half and draw a line through the bottom. {@secretary} looks relieved. {@group_leader} calls Friday and is told the bill paragraph did not fit, which is not a lie the way you said it. She knows. The diapers come in by the carload.

choices.label: Run the whole page, the representatives' names and votes included
choices.outcome: It prints. Someone sends it to one of the named representatives, who sends it to the chancery with a note about electioneering. {@chancellor} calls {@pastor}, who was at a deanery meeting and had never seen it. The group frames the page. You spend a week apologizing to a man who did not want to be apologized to.

choices.label: Hold the bulletin an hour and call {@pastor} out of his meeting
choices.outcome: He answers on the fourth try and says, in the tone of a man in a hallway, that nothing goes in the bulletin with a legislator's name in it and that you should have known that. The insert runs with the diaper drive alone. {@secretary} pays the rush fee out of petty cash and does not forget it.

events.title: The Speaker
events.body: The pro-life group has booked a speaker for the hall: a woman who runs a pregnancy center two counties over and who is also, it turns out when you look her up, a candidate for the state house. The flyer went up in the vestibule before anyone in the rectory saw it. {@group_leader} says it is about the center and the center's work, and that what the woman does on her own time is her business, and she may even believe that. The talk is in nine days. {@pastor} is away on retreat and left you the keys and the sentence use your judgment, which he says when he does not want to be called. The parish is not permitted to host candidates as candidates. It is permitted to host anyone as anything else. The line between those is a matter of what is said from the front of the hall, and you will not be the one saying it.
events.flavorPrompt: A flyer already on the wall, a pastor on retreat, a line that exists on paper and nowhere else.

choices.label: Host it, introduce her yourself, and set the terms from the podium
choices.outcome: You introduce her as the director of a pregnancy center and say, before she speaks, that the parish is honored to hear about the center's work and takes no position on any election. She keeps to it, mostly. Someone in the back asks about her race and she says come find me afterward. {@group_leader} thought the introduction was unnecessary and says so.

choices.label: Cancel the hall booking until after the election
choices.outcome: The flyer comes down. {@group_leader} calls it censorship to the group and to two other parishes' groups, one of which hosts the talk instead. You are named in a newsletter as the priest who would not let a pro-life woman speak. It is not accurate. It is not going anywhere either.

choices.label: Give them the keys and stay in the rectory
choices.outcome: You are told afterward it was a good talk about the center and a bad talk about the legislature, in that order. A parishioner who works for the county posts about it. {@pastor} returns from retreat to a voicemail from {@chancellor} and asks you what use your judgment meant to you.

events.title: The Car in the Back Lot
events.body: The Vincentians do their home visits in pairs and write them up in a ledger nobody reads but them. {@group_leader} brings you a page from it after the Tuesday meeting and asks you to read it where no one else can. A mother and two children have been sleeping in a car in the parish's back lot for nine nights. The conference has been bringing them food. The mother asked them not to tell the parish office. Her brother is a parishioner. Her brother is the man whose family's name is on the hall, whose envelope carries the second collection most months, and who has told her, she says, that she made her bed. The Vincentians can get her into a shelter program with a referral from the parish. The referral form has a line for the pastor's signature. {@group_leader} has not shown the page to {@pastor} because she is afraid he will call the brother first, and she thinks that is the wrong order.
events.flavorPrompt: A ledger page, a back lot, and a name on a building. Write the poverty as ordinary and the money as the thing everyone is tiptoeing around.

choices.label: Sign the referral yourself as parochial vicar and tell {@pastor} after
choices.outcome: Your signature is good enough for the county. The family is in the program by Friday. {@pastor} finds out the following week when the brother calls him, and he is angrier that he was told second than about anything else. The brother's envelope is lighter for a season. {@group_leader} would follow you anywhere now.

choices.label: Take the page to {@pastor} with {@group_leader} beside you
choices.outcome: He reads it twice and, to her visible surprise, does not reach for the phone. He signs the referral. Then he calls the brother, and the conversation is short and not warm, and the brother's family sits at the 11:00 the next Sunday without looking at the front. {@pastor} says to you afterward that he is not a fool, and you believe him.

choices.label: Find her a place through a friend at another parish. Keep {parish} out of it
choices.outcome: {@closest_classmate}'s parish has a conference with a house. The family goes there. No form crosses {@pastor}'s desk and the brother is never told. {@group_leader} is grateful and a little disappointed; she wanted the parish to be the one that helped. The ledger page goes back in the ledger.

choices.label: Tell her it is the conference's work and the conference should handle it
choices.outcome: She hears you say that the priests will not touch it, and she is not wrong. The Vincentians find the family a motel for two weeks with their own funds and then lose track of them. {@group_leader} does not bring you a ledger page again.

events.title: A Visit With a Collar
events.body: The Vincentians go out in twos, and this week one of the twos has asked for a priest. The man they visit is dying slowly in a second-floor apartment with a niece who works nights, and he has stopped answering the door for anyone but them. He was a parishioner once. He has not been to Mass in twenty years and told {@group_leader}, the last time, that he would not know what to say to a priest and a priest would not know what to say to him. She thinks that is the reason to send one. The visit is Thursday afternoon, which is when you write, and it will take the afternoon, because the Vincentians do not leave when the food is delivered. They sit. It is the whole point of them. You would bring the oils, in case, and not mention them unless asked.
events.flavorPrompt: Plain and quiet. An apartment, a niece's shift schedule, a man who has not been to Mass in twenty years. No conversion scene.

choices.label: Go with them Thursday
choices.outcome: He does not want to talk about God and you do not make him. You talk about the building, which used to be a good building. On the stairs down {@group_leader} says he asked her to bring you back. The afternoon is gone and the homily is Saturday's problem.

choices.label: Send word that he can call the rectory any time. Keep Thursday
choices.outcome: He does not call the rectory. The Vincentians keep going on Thursdays with the bag of groceries and the hour of sitting. Three months later {@group_leader} tells you, in the hallway after the meeting, that he died on a Tuesday, and that the niece asked whether a priest had ever come. She says she told her the truth, and she does not say it unkindly, which is worse.

events.title: The Poor Box
events.body: The St. Vincent de Paul conference keeps its own account, by rule and by the Society's own governance: the poor box, the special collections, the checks from the estate lawyers who know where to send them. It is not the parish's money. This is a point that pastors understand in the abstract. {@pastor} has an invoice on his desk that is due before the next assessment and a conference account with eleven thousand dollars in it, and he has asked {@group_leader}, in a tone she describes to you as friendly, whether the Society could see its way to a short loan. She has come to you because you are the priest who is not him. The Society's rule is clear. The pastor is the pastor. The poor are, at the moment, not in the room. {@group_leader} would like you to tell her what to do, and you know she will do what you say, which is the worst part.
events.flavorPrompt: A rule, a pastor, and eleven thousand dollars that belongs to people who are not present. Keep the pastor human.

choices.label: Tell her the rule is the rule, and tell {@pastor} you told her
choices.outcome: She says no to him with your name attached. He does not argue, which is either grace or the long game. The invoice gets paid from somewhere worse. The conference's treasurer sends you a Christmas card for the first time.

choices.label: Broker it: a written loan, a repayment date, the conference's council informed
choices.outcome: You draft a one-page agreement, insist the conference's district council sign off, and set a date. {@pastor} finds the formality irritating and signs it. The money moves and comes back on schedule, which surprises {@group_leader} more than it should. The Society's district office notes that {parish} did it properly.

choices.label: Tell her the pastor is the pastor
choices.outcome: The money moves without paper. The invoice is paid. Repayment is discussed and then not discussed. Six months later the conference cannot cover a family's rent and {@group_leader} does not look at you when she tells the meeting why. You hear the word borrowed in the parking lot, in quotation marks.

effects.value: Conference funds moved to the parish without paper

events.title: Fish Fry Friday
events.body: The Knights' Lenten fish fry is the best-attended thing {parish} does that is not a Mass, and some Fridays it is closer than anyone likes to admit. Seven Fridays, four hundred dinners each, cash at the door and a jar for the beer. The council has always split the proceeds with the parish; the split has always been whatever the Grand Knight said it was. This year {@group_leader} has announced, at the first Friday, that the council is putting the money toward a new kitchen for the hall, which the parish needs and which the parish would then own. {@pastor} was counting the fish fry toward the assessment. He has asked you, because the Knights like you, to find out what the number actually is. Nobody has seen a ledger. The council's treasurer is a retired man who keeps the books in a spiral notebook, and the notebook is in his truck.
events.flavorPrompt: Fried fish, a spiral notebook, and money that has never once been counted in front of a priest. Genial and opaque.

choices.label: Ask the treasurer, nicely, for the notebook
choices.outcome: He brings it to the rectory Monday and it is more careful than you expected and less than it should be. The number is real and large. {@group_leader} takes the request as an insult on the council's behalf and says so at the next Friday, loudly, near the fryers. The parish gets its share, and the council gets a story about you.

choices.label: Offer to do the council's books for them this Lent
choices.outcome: You sit at the door with a cash box and a receipt pad for seven Fridays. The number, counted, is a third higher than the notebook ever said, because the jar was never counted at all. The council is embarrassed and then proud. The kitchen gets funded and the parish gets the rest, and {@group_leader} calls you the council's chaplain without asking whether you want the title.

choices.label: Side with the council: the kitchen is a better use than the assessment
choices.outcome: You tell {@pastor} the Knights are building him a kitchen and he should let them. He says the diocese does not accept kitchens. The council loves you. The assessment is paid late with a note from the chancery's finance office that {@pastor} reads aloud at a staff meeting, looking at you.

events.title: Pancakes
events.body: The Knights' pancake breakfast is after the 9:00 on Sunday and {@group_leader} has asked, as he asks every month, whether Father would say grace and stay for a plate. It is a small thing. It is also the one hour a month when the men of the parish who do not otherwise talk to a priest will talk to one, over syrup, about their knees and their sons. {@pastor} used to go and now sends you. There is a new banner to bless, a Fourth Degree member's anniversary to acknowledge, and a raffle you will be asked to draw. The 11:00 is yours. You can do the grace and leave. You can stay and be late to the sacristy. You can send {@secretary} down with a note, which the men will read for exactly what it is.
events.flavorPrompt: Syrup, a banner, and a room of men who talk sideways. The smallness is the point.

choices.label: Say grace, bless the banner, and go vest
choices.outcome: You are in and out in twelve minutes. {@group_leader} thanks you as if you had stayed an hour, which is the Knights' way. Two of the men catch you in the hallway after the 11:00 to finish the conversation you did not have.

choices.label: Stay for a plate and be late to the sacristy
choices.outcome: You hear about two knees, a son in the Navy, and a marriage that is quieter than it used to be. You vest with syrup on your cuff and start the 11:00 four minutes late. {@pastor} notices. So does the man with the quiet marriage, who comes to confession the next Saturday for the first time in years.

choices.label: Send a note down with the secretary
choices.outcome: The note is read aloud, kindly, by {@group_leader}, over the syrup, and the men nod at it as they would nod at a bulletin announcement. It is not the same as a priest at the table and everyone in the hall knows it. The following month he does not ask, and you notice that he does not ask, and you do not go down on your own.

events.title: A Plaque the Size of a Door
events.body: The council has voted to give the parish twenty thousand dollars toward the building's worst problem, and {@group_leader} brings the news to you first, at the pancake breakfast, because he wants you to be the one who tells {@pastor}. There are terms. The council wants a plaque in the vestibule. It wants the Knights' emblem on the plaque, at a size he indicates with his hands. It wants the council's name read at the announcements for a month. And it wants, though this is said more softly, a standing agreement that the council's meetings take precedence in the hall on Tuesday nights, which is the night the young adults meet and the night the Spanish choir rehearses. Twenty thousand dollars is a real number in {parish}. So is a vestibule. {@pastor} has said before that he does not sell wall space. He has also said, more recently, that he does not know how he is going to pay for the repair.
events.flavorPrompt: Generosity with a shape to it. The plaque is the real object; measure it with the leader's hands.

choices.label: Carry the whole offer to {@pastor} and recommend he take it
choices.outcome: He takes it. The plaque goes up and is, in fairness, handsome. The Tuesday night arrangement is the part nobody wrote down and everybody remembers. The young adults move to Wednesdays and lose a third of their people. The council has never been more visible or more pleased.

choices.label: Take the money and the plaque. Refuse the Tuesdays
choices.outcome: You tell {@group_leader} the plaque is a memorial and the hall is a schedule and the parish does not trade one for the other. He is put out, then reasonable. The gift comes with the plaque and without the Tuesdays. {@pastor} says you handled it and means it, which from him is a paragraph.

choices.label: Tell him gifts with terms are not gifts, and the parish will manage
choices.outcome: The council withdraws the offer and gives the money instead to the diocesan seminary fund, where it is acknowledged with a letter and no plaque. {@pastor} hears the number you turned down and does not speak to you for two days. The Tuesday nights remain what they were.

events.title: The May Crowning
events.body: The guild has crowned the statue of Our Lady on the first Sunday of May for as long as anyone can find a photograph, and the photographs go back to hats. The hymn has always been the same hymn. {@music_director} has programmed something else this year, a setting from the new repertoire that the choir has been rehearsing for a month, and has told {@group_leader} that the old hymn is theologically thin and musically worse. {@group_leader} has told {@music_director} that the guild will process in silence before it processes to that. Both of them have now told you, separately, at length, and each has ended with the sentence that {@pastor} will not deal with it, which is true; he has dealt with it by scheduling a funeral for himself that morning. The crowning is in nine days. The guild irons the altar linens, runs the funeral luncheons, and has eleven women who have not missed a daily Mass in a decade. The choir has eight paid section leaders and a director on contract.
events.flavorPrompt: Two competent people who cannot both be right, and a pastor who has fled. The hymn matters to everyone in the scene and the prose should not mock that.

choices.label: The old hymn. It is the guild's crowning
choices.outcome: You tell {@music_director} that a custom is a form of liturgy and that the guild's is older than his contract. He plays it, badly on purpose. {@group_leader} cries during the procession, which she does every year. The choir's section leaders send a note about respect that {@pastor} reads and files.

choices.label: The new setting. He is the music director and it is his loft
choices.outcome: The setting is beautiful and nobody in the guild sings it. They process in silence, as promised, and it is a longer silence than you had imagined. {@music_director} is grateful in the way of a man who has won something he will now have to keep. Two of the eleven daily Mass women stop ironing the linens. The linens are noticed.

choices.label: Both: the guild sings the old hymn in procession, the choir sings the setting at the crowning
choices.outcome: It takes three conversations and one lie about the other party's flexibility. The guild sings coming in and the choir sings at the statue, and the crowning runs eleven minutes long, and everyone is unhappy for exactly as long as it takes to reach the coffee. {@pastor}, back from his funeral, asks how you did that and you tell him.

choices.label: Tell them both the pastor decides, and put it in writing on his desk
choices.outcome: He reads your memo, sighs, and picks the old hymn without meeting anyone. {@music_director} concludes you were behind it. {@group_leader} concludes you were no help. The crowning proceeds as it always has and you have made two enemies out of one decision you did not make.

events.title: Ham and Rolls
events.body: The funeral is Thursday. The family has asked for the guild's luncheon in the hall afterward, ham and rolls and the good coffee urn, which the guild has done for every funeral at {parish} since before the hall had a kitchen. {@group_leader} has told {@secretary} the guild will not be serving. The reason, when you get it out of her, is that the family has asked {@music_director}'s ensemble to sing, and the guild's position is that it does not serve luncheons at ensemble funerals. It is the first time this position has existed. It is also, you understand as she says it, a position she is prepared to hold. The family does not know any of this. They know their mother is dead and that there was supposed to be ham. {@music_director} has been told and is, he says, entirely relaxed about it, which he is not. The luncheon is in two days and the guild owns the urn.
events.flavorPrompt: A grief the parish is supposed to serve, made hostage to a feud the parish is supposed to be above. Keep the family offstage and real.

choices.label: Tell her the family did not choose the ensemble to hurt her, and ask her to serve for the mother
choices.outcome: She serves. She does not speak to {@music_director} in the hall, which is a thing she has practice at. The family never knows. {@group_leader} tells you afterward that she did it for you, which is what she wants you to owe her.

choices.label: Have the parish cater it and let the guild sit this one out
choices.outcome: The catered ham is fine. The rolls are wrong. Someone in the family notices the urn is not the good urn. {@group_leader} hears that the parish went around her and takes it as the message it is. {@music_director} says nothing and looks pleased.

choices.label: Ask the family, delicately, whether the parish choir might sing instead
choices.outcome: The family says yes because they say yes to everything this week. The guild serves. {@music_director} learns that his ensemble was removed from a funeral by the vicar and takes it to {@pastor} in writing, with the word undermined. The ham is excellent.

events.title: The Sacristy Key
events.body: {@group_leader} has had a key to the sacristy for twenty-two years. She uses it on Saturday mornings to change the linens, count the hosts, and rearrange whatever the previous week's servers left crooked. {@maintenance} has changed the locks after the second time the side door was found open overnight, and has issued new keys to the staff and to the priests and not to the guild. She has come to you rather than to him, because he is a man who says no and you are, she has decided, a priest who says yes. The sacristy is yours in a way it is not hers. It is also cleaner because of her than it would be because of you. {@pastor} is aware of the lock change and of nothing else, which is how he prefers it.
events.flavorPrompt: A small territorial matter with a long history. Keys as a form of belonging.

choices.label: Get her a key from {@maintenance} and take the argument
choices.outcome: {@maintenance} gives you the key with the face of a man who will remember this the next time a door is left open. {@group_leader} carries it on a ribbon. The sacristy is spotless. The side door is, as far as anyone knows, never her doing.

choices.label: Meet her Saturday mornings and unlock it yourself
choices.outcome: You are in the sacristy at seven every Saturday, which you had not planned. She talks while she folds. In a month you know more about the parish from her than from {@pastor} in a year. {@maintenance} keeps his locks and his peace.

choices.label: Back {@maintenance}. The locks are the locks
choices.outcome: She says she understands, in the voice of a woman who has understood pastors for forty years, and stops changing the linens. They are changed by whoever notices, which is sometimes nobody. {@maintenance} nods at you in the hallway, which is what he has instead of thanks. The sacristy is yours now, and it looks it.

events.title: The Tuesday Group
events.body: The Tuesday Bible study meets in the library with the door closed, and for a year you have taken that for a good sign. {@group_leader} runs it well. The attendance has doubled. This month you learn why: they have set aside the diocesan program and are watching a video series by a priest from another state whose bishop removed his faculties last spring. The series is about the Book of Revelation, the current pontificate, and the end of things, in that order. The videos are slick and the priest is a gifted speaker. {@group_leader} says the group finds the diocesan program shallow, which it is. She says the group is grown adults who can weigh what they hear, which they are. She says {@pastor} does not need to know, which is the sentence that brought her to your office. You have read enough to know exactly what is wrong with the series and enough to know that saying so will sound like a man defending his guild.
events.flavorPrompt: A closed library door, a slick video, and a leader who is not stupid. The pull of a better teacher than the diocese offers.

choices.label: Offer to teach Revelation yourself for the next eight weeks
choices.outcome: It costs you Tuesday nights and a week of preparation you did not have. The group is skeptical and then, by the fourth week, not. Half the room has never heard the text read as literature and liturgy rather than prophecy. Two people leave for the video priest anyway. {@group_leader} says you are better than the videos and does not say she has stopped watching them.

choices.label: Tell her the series is off the table in a parish building, and tell {@pastor} why
choices.outcome: She hears the word forbidden even though you did not use it. {@pastor} backs you flatly and without interest. The group meets the next Tuesday at a member's house with the video on, and the library is empty. The parish has kept its building clean and lost its Bible study.

choices.label: Let grown adults weigh what they hear. Do not tell {@pastor}
choices.outcome: The group keeps growing. By Advent three of them have stopped receiving Communion from {@pastor} on principle, and one of them tells him why in the sacristy. He asks you whether you knew. You tell him. He says that you are a priest of {diocese} and not a librarian, and leaves it there, where it stays.

effects.value: Let a Bible study follow a priest without faculties

choices.label: Come on Tuesday, watch the video with them, and take it apart afterward
choices.outcome: You sit through forty minutes of it, which is worse than reading about it. Then you take the three central claims and show, with the text open, what each one does with the text. It lands with about half the room. The other half decides you are an academic and not a pastor, and says so at coffee. {@group_leader} sets the series aside for now.

events.title: The Prologue
events.body: The Bible study is starting John and {@group_leader} would like a priest for the first session, because the prologue frightens people and she would rather someone with a degree stood in front of it. It is a Tuesday evening, ninety minutes, twelve people with the diocesan workbook open to a page that says In the beginning was the Word and then asks what that means to you. You know what it means. You spent a semester on it. Whether you can say it to a retired nurse and a man who drives for the county in a way that leaves them with something is a different question and the one that matters. {@pastor} has not been to a Bible study in the years anyone can count. The group notices that. It notices everything, quietly, with the workbook open.
events.flavorPrompt: A workbook, a prologue, and twelve adults. Teaching as a form of pastoral care.

choices.label: Go, and teach the prologue
choices.outcome: You do it without notes and it is better than the workbook. The county driver asks whether the Word was there before the Father and you spend twenty minutes on it and he goes home satisfied. {@group_leader} asks whether you would come back for chapter six.

choices.label: Send her three pages of notes and let her lead it
choices.outcome: She reads your notes aloud, which is not what you meant. They are good notes. The group thanks you through her. It is the difference between a letter and a visit and everyone in the room knows which they received.

events.title: Twenty-Four Hours
events.body: The adoration guild wants perpetual adoration: the Blessed Sacrament exposed in the day chapel around the clock, every hour covered by at least one adorer, the doors unlocked at three in the morning for whoever holds the three o'clock. {@group_leader} has the sign-up sheet already, with a hundred and forty names and every hour covered but four. She has the monstrance picked out. She has, she says, prayed about this for two years. The diocesan risk office has answered {@pastor}'s inquiry with a letter that says the parish's coverage does not extend to an unlocked building overnight with a single unaccompanied person in it, and that the chapel would need a keypad, a camera, and a second adorer at every hour after ten. That is a hundred and forty more names and about nine thousand dollars. {@pastor} has handed you the letter and the sheet and said you seem to be the one she talks to.
events.flavorPrompt: A sign-up sheet with a hundred and forty names against a letter from an insurer. Both are serious documents.

choices.label: Raise the nine thousand and fill the hours. Make it happen
choices.outcome: It takes four months, two second collections, and a keypad you learn to hate. The chapel opens on a feast day. At three in the morning in February there are two people in it, one of them asleep, and the light is on in a building that used to be dark. {@group_leader} has become the most powerful layperson in the parish, and she knows it.

choices.label: Offer exposition from six to ten daily, doors locked after. Half of what she asked
choices.outcome: She takes it as a defeat and then, month by month, as a practice. The chapel is full at six-thirty. The hundred and forty names become sixty who come. {@group_leader} does not stop asking about the nights. {@pastor} says you found the right size for it and is, for once, right.

choices.label: Tell her the letter is the answer and the parish cannot afford the rest
choices.outcome: She says the parish could afford it if it wanted to, and produces the fish fry number, which she should not have. The guild's meetings shrink. The sign-up sheet stays on the bulletin board for a year, names fading, until {@secretary} takes it down.

events.title: The Empty Hour
events.body: The adoration guild covers the chapel from the early Mass until evening, and lately the eleven-to-midnight hour has had nobody in it. {@group_leader} has asked around and gotten the answers people give: work, children, a husband who does not like the drive. She asks you. She asks, she says, because the guild would be ashamed to repose the Sacrament early on a weekday when the parish has two priests in the rectory a hundred feet away. It is an hour. It is also eleven at night, every Wednesday, indefinitely, and you know exactly what the following Thursday morning feels like when you have kept it. {@pastor} used to take an hour in the chapel and no longer does, and she has not asked him.
events.flavorPrompt: A quiet ask at the edge of the day. The chapel at eleven as a real place, cold and lit.

choices.label: Take the hour
choices.outcome: You take it. The chapel at eleven is cold and the kneeler is bad and it is, most weeks, the only hour you have prayed without an agenda. {@group_leader} does not thank you, because she thinks it was owed. Thursday mornings are slower.

choices.label: Find her two people from the men's Mass and stay out of the chapel
choices.outcome: You ask from the pulpit and two men you have never spoken to sign up together. The hour is covered. {@group_leader} would rather it had been you, and says the men are very faithful in a voice that means something else.

choices.label: Tell her to repose at ten on Wednesdays. It is not a failure
choices.outcome: She reposes at ten on Wednesdays, and it is not a failure, and she does not agree. The guild's monthly letter to its members notes the change without comment, which is its comment. Two of the older adorers take it as a sign of the parish's direction and say so at the eight o'clock. The chapel is dark an hour earlier than it was.

events.title: The Hymnal
events.body: The pew hymnals are falling apart and {@pastor} has budgeted to replace them. That was the easy part. {@music_director} has recommended one publisher's hardbound edition: mostly contemporary, a strong psalter, the old hymns in a back section. {@group_leader}, who has led the choir through three directors, has circulated a petition among the choir for a different book: chant settings, the traditional repertoire, and a Latin ordinary the choir has never sung. Both of them have come to you because {@pastor} has said, in the parking lot, that he will buy whichever one the vicar recommends, since the vicar will be the one singing out of it longest. It is nine thousand dollars either way. It is also, everyone understands, a decision about what {parish} is going to sound like for fifteen years, and the choir will be the ones who sing it or refuse to.
events.flavorPrompt: Two catalogs and a parking-lot delegation. A liturgical decision disguised as a purchase order.

choices.label: The director's book
choices.outcome: The books arrive in a truck and smell of glue. {@music_director} programs the new repertoire and the assembly, within a season, sings more than it did. {@group_leader} leads the choir through it and does not forgive you. Three altos leave for the parish across the river with the Latin ordinary.

choices.label: The choir's book
choices.outcome: The choir learns the Latin ordinary in a month and sings it at the Easter Vigil, and it is, {@pastor} says afterward, the best they have ever sounded. The assembly does not sing the chant. {@music_director} updates his résumé. {@group_leader} has won and knows what it cost you.

choices.label: Neither. A subscription missalette for a year and a decision after you have heard them both
choices.outcome: The missalettes are ugly and cheap and nobody likes them, which is the point. For a year the choir sings from both catalogs and the parish hears what it is choosing between. {@pastor} thinks you dodged it. {@group_leader} and {@music_director} think so too, and are, for the first time, in agreement.

events.title: Lessons and Carols
events.body: The choir's Advent concert is the third Sunday at four, and {@group_leader} would like a priest to read the lessons between the carols, in an alb, from the ambo, in the voice you use for the Gospel. It is an hour and a half. It is the same afternoon the school's Christmas pageant is in the hall and {@pastor} is at the pageant because the school is his; he has said, without saying it, that the choir is yours. The concert is the choir's one public thing, and it is the one afternoon a year the choir is the reason people come to {parish} rather than the thing they hear while they are there. The nine lessons are long. The church will be cold. Half the audience will be Protestant neighbors, which is a thing the choir is proud of and the parish forgets.
events.flavorPrompt: A cold church at four in the afternoon in December, and a choir that is briefly the center of something.

choices.label: Read the lessons
choices.outcome: You read nine lessons in a cold church and the choir sings between them, and it is, in fact, beautiful. Two of the Protestant neighbors come to Midnight Mass. {@group_leader} gives you a card signed by the whole choir, and you keep it.

choices.label: Ask a deacon to read. Go to the pageant with {@pastor}
choices.outcome: The deacon reads well. {@pastor} is surprised to see you at the pageant and not displeased. The choir notices that neither priest came to the one afternoon that was theirs, and {@group_leader} says nothing about it for a long time, and then, once, something.

events.title: Six Weeks to the Vigil
events.body: {@group_leader} brings you the file of a candidate for full communion, a woman baptized Presbyterian who has come every Tuesday since September, married to a parishioner, and, as of the intake form she filled out in the fall and nobody read closely, married once before. The first marriage ended in divorce eleven years ago. There is no declaration of nullity and no one has filed for one. The Easter Vigil is in six weeks. If she is received at the Vigil in a marriage the Church does not recognize, she will be admitted to Communion on Holy Saturday night and, strictly, barred from it on Easter Sunday morning. {@group_leader} is heartbroken on the woman's behalf and, underneath that, on the team's; the form was on her desk in October. {@pastor} has said the tribunal takes fourteen months and the woman can be received next year. The woman has not been told anything yet. Her husband is a lector.
events.flavorPrompt: A file, a form nobody read, and a woman who has done everything asked of her. The canon law is real and the prose should not apologize for it or hide behind it.

choices.label: Ask about the first husband before assuming a fourteen-month case
choices.outcome: You sit with her and ask, gently, about the first wedding. It was at a courthouse. The first husband was a baptized Catholic. That is a lack of canonical form, not a formal case: a documentary process, weeks with the right paperwork, not months. The tribunal confirms it in nineteen days. She is received at the Vigil. {@group_leader} says you saved it, and you say the tribunal did.

choices.label: Tell her the truth yourself, this week, and walk with her through the year
choices.outcome: She cries and then asks what she has to do. You tell her, and you tell her you will be at every Tuesday until it is done. She keeps coming. Her husband stops lectoring for a season and then starts again. The following Vigil she is received, and the team weeps, and {@group_leader} reads every form now.

choices.label: Receive her at the Vigil and sort out the paperwork after
choices.outcome: She is received in a white scarf with the others and does not know anything was wrong. {@pastor} finds out in May from the tribunal's intake clerk, who is a parishioner. He does not shout. He says that you have made him a liar to the tribunal and that he will not forget it. The woman receives Communion every Sunday. The file is open.

effects.value: Received a candidate in an unregularized marriage

choices.label: It is {@pastor}'s decision and his conversation. Let him have it
choices.outcome: He tells her, briskly, after a Tuesday session, in the hallway. She does not come back. Her husband stops lectoring. {@group_leader} blames herself and, without saying it, you, for not being the one in the hallway. The team loses two members by summer.

events.title: The Session on the Eucharist
events.body: The RCIA team runs its own sessions from the diocesan outline and does it competently, but {@group_leader} has a standing request that a priest teach the night on the Eucharist, because the catechumens ask questions on that night that the team does not want to answer wrong. It is a Tuesday from seven to nine in the library. There are nine of them this year: two teenagers, a couple marrying in June, a man in his sixties whose wife died Catholic, and four others whose stories you have not learned. The team will have coffee. They will have, {@group_leader} warns you, the question about whether the bread is still bread, from the man in his sixties, who asks it every week of everyone. {@pastor} has done this night for years and has asked you to take it, not as a favor.
events.flavorPrompt: A library, nine adults, and the one question that always comes. Catechesis as a conversation.

choices.label: Teach it
choices.outcome: The man in his sixties asks whether it is still bread and you tell him no, and then you tell him why, for half an hour, and he is quiet afterward in a way {@group_leader} says he has not been. Two of the nine ask about confession. It is nine-forty when you lock the library.

choices.label: Send them the diocesan video and take the questions by email
choices.outcome: The diocesan video is fine, and the team runs the discussion from its outline. The man in his sixties emails you four hundred words about bread the next morning, and you answer him well, and he is grateful. {@group_leader} does not ask you again that year. The nine of them are received at the Vigil by a priest they have seen only from the pews.

events.title: The Couple Who Will Not Come
events.body: The wedding is booked for October, the deposit paid, the church reserved by the bride's mother in a phone call to {@secretary} that did not mention the couple. The couple lives in another state. They have missed two Pre-Cana weekends and the inventory session, and {@group_leader}, who runs the team with her husband and has for nine years, has told you she will not sign off on a couple she has never met. The bride's mother has called {@pastor} twice. {@pastor} has told you to handle it, which means either the team bends or the mother is told no, and he would rather not be the one for either. The diocese requires six months and a program. The program is the team. The team is {@group_leader}. The bride has emailed you, once, to say they are very busy and very much in love, and could they do it over video.
events.flavorPrompt: A mother, a deposit, and a team leader who has been doing this longer than the vicar has been ordained. Nobody is wrong and nobody is present.

choices.label: Back {@group_leader}. No program, no wedding here
choices.outcome: The mother calls the chancery, which calls {@pastor}, who calls you, who says the same thing again. The couple does the program at a parish near where they live and sends the certificate. The wedding is in October. {@group_leader} would take a bullet for you now, and the mother would fire it.

choices.label: Do the preparation with them yourself, over video, four evenings
choices.outcome: You talk to two strangers on a screen about money and children and the Church and what each thinks the other wants. It is better than you expected and worse than the weekend. {@group_leader} signs the form because you ask her to and says the team is not a rubber stamp. The couple marries in October. You could not pick them out of the congregation.

choices.label: Have {@pastor} sign the dispensation from the program. It is his to give
choices.outcome: He signs it because you asked and because the mother's family has a pew. {@group_leader} resigns from the team by letter, nine years and four hundred couples, and her husband with her. The team does not recover that year. The wedding is lovely.

events.title: The Inventory
events.body: The marriage preparation team runs the premarital inventory on a Saturday morning for the spring's couples: a long questionnaire, a scored report, and an afternoon of conversation about where the scores disagree. It takes four sponsor couples and this year {@group_leader} has three. The fourth couple has a sick parent. She has asked whether you would take the fourth table: two couples, three hours, a report you have been trained to read and never actually used. She has asked {@pastor} in previous years and he has done it, grumbling, and this year he has a wedding at one. The couples at the fourth table are a nurse and a mechanic who have been living together for four years, and two graduate students who have not, and who are, {@group_leader} says, terrified of the money questions.
events.flavorPrompt: A Saturday morning in the hall with a scored questionnaire. Married life as something two strangers are trying to describe to you.

choices.label: Take the fourth table
choices.outcome: The nurse and the mechanic disagree about children and did not know it until the report said so, and you spend most of the three hours there. The graduate students are fine about money and afraid of everything else. {@group_leader} says you did well for a celibate, which is the team's joke and also its question.

choices.label: Have her reschedule the two couples for the next session
choices.outcome: The nurse and the mechanic move their wedding to another parish that had a Saturday, because the date mattered more than the building. The graduate students wait for the next session and are, {@group_leader} says, fine. She does not say anything about the fourth table, and the next session has four sponsor couples and no vicar, and she has not asked for one.

events.title: The Tuition Letter
events.body: The school's tuition letter goes out in February and this year it carries a nine percent increase, which the finance council approved in a meeting the parents were not at. {@group_leader}, who chairs the parent association and has three children in the building, has asked for a meeting in the hall with a priest present, and {@pastor} has sent you, because he chairs the finance council and would rather not sit across from it. Sixty parents come. The numbers are not complicated: the parish subsidy has not grown, enrollment has dropped by eleven, the teachers have not had a raise in four years and two have left for the public district. {@group_leader} has a proposal. The association will run a capital appeal if the parish freezes tuition for a year and covers the gap. The gap is about forty thousand dollars. The parish does not have forty thousand dollars; it has a boiler. You have a microphone and sixty people who love the school and are doing the arithmetic in their heads.
events.flavorPrompt: A hall, sixty parents, and arithmetic. Nobody is greedy. The school as the parish's most beloved and most expensive object.

choices.label: Walk them through the numbers honestly and refuse to promise what the parish does not have
choices.outcome: You put the subsidy, the enrollment, and the teachers' pay on the screen and let it sit. Nobody likes it. Nobody argues with it. {@group_leader} says afterward that she wishes {@pastor} had done that a year ago. The appeal goes ahead anyway, smaller. Four families withdraw. The teachers stay.

choices.label: Back the freeze publicly and take it to {@pastor} as the parents' priest
choices.outcome: The room applauds. {@pastor} does not. He tells you the finance council is not a suggestion box and that you have promised sixty people money you do not control. He freezes it anyway, for a year, because the alternative is now worse. The boiler waits. {@group_leader} runs the appeal and it raises a little more than half.

choices.label: Propose a tiered tuition with a real audit of who pays what
choices.outcome: You have looked at the ledger and a third of the families pay a discounted rate nobody has reviewed in a decade. You propose a tiered schedule with a means form. It is unpopular with the third and persuasive to the rest. {@pastor} adopts it. Enrollment holds. {@group_leader} is not sure whether you helped the school or the parish and decides, provisionally, both.

events.title: The Gala
events.body: The parent association's spring gala is at a hotel ballroom on a Saturday night: a silent auction, a paddle raise, a band that plays until eleven, and a priest at the head table in a collar, because the donors like to see one. {@pastor} has gone for nineteen years and has told {@group_leader} that this year the vicar will represent the parish, which she has told you, with a tone that suggests it is a promotion. It is not a small evening. The gala is a third of the school's fundraising and the association's whole year. The paddle raise goes better when the priest stands up first. You have the vigil Mass at five and would be at the hotel by seven, and you have never once known what to say to a man who has just paid four thousand dollars for a week at someone's lake house.
events.flavorPrompt: A ballroom, a paddle raise, and a priest in a collar being looked at. Mildly comic and entirely necessary.

choices.label: Go, sit at the head table, and stand up first for the paddle raise
choices.outcome: You stand up first and say a number that is more than you should, and the room follows. The band is loud. A man who bought the lake house week tells you about his mother's funeral for twenty minutes. {@group_leader} is radiant. Sunday morning you are tired in the way that has nothing to say for itself.

choices.label: Go for the blessing and the first hour, then leave
choices.outcome: You bless the meal, shake forty hands, and are gone before the paddle raise, which goes fine without you and a little softer than last year. {@group_leader} says she understands, in the voice of someone updating a list. The following year {@pastor} goes again, nineteen years and one, and does not mention why.

choices.label: Send regrets. It is not a priest's evening
choices.outcome: {@group_leader} reads your regrets at the head table with no priest at it. The paddle raise is soft. She tells {@pastor} the parish was not represented, and he tells you, and it is the first time you hear him use the word represented as a verb that applies to you.

events.title: One O'Clock
events.body: The community's Mass is at one on Sunday afternoon, which is the hour left over after the parish's Masses, and it is the fullest Mass of the day. {@group_leader} has come with a delegation of six to ask that it be moved to eleven, and that the English eleven, which draws eighty people to a church that seats six hundred, move to one. He has the counts. He has had them for two years. He says, without heat, that the community pays into the collection like anyone, cleans the hall after its own feasts, and is tired of being the Mass that gets the parking lot after the others have left it. {@pastor} has said the eleven is the eleven, and the people at the eleven have been at the eleven since they were baptized in it. The delegation has come to you because you are younger and, {@group_leader} says, because you look like a man who has not yet decided who the parish is for.
events.flavorPrompt: Six people in an office with attendance counts. The Mass schedule as the real map of a parish's heart. Keep both congregations human.

choices.label: Take the counts to {@pastor} and argue for the swap
choices.outcome: He looks at the numbers he has always known and says the eleven is not about numbers. You say a parish is. He does not move the Mass that year. He does move it the year after, when the eighty have become sixty. {@group_leader} remembers who carried the paper in. So do the sixty.

choices.label: Propose one bilingual eleven o'clock for both, and offer to preach it
choices.outcome: Neither side wants it and {@pastor}, for reasons of his own, lets you try it for Lent. You preach in two languages badly and then less badly. Half the eighty stay. Most of the community comes. It is not the swap and it is not nothing, and at the sign of peace two congregations who have shared a building for a decade meet each other for the first time.

choices.label: Tell them the eleven belongs to the people who built the church
choices.outcome: {@group_leader} thanks you for your time in a voice that has closed a door. The delegation does not come back. The one o'clock stays full and the community begins, quietly, to talk about the parish across the highway with the Mass at ten. {@pastor} is relieved. You are not sure what you have kept.

events.title: The Procession
events.body: The community's patronal feast falls on a Saturday this year and {@group_leader} has asked to process from the church through the neighborhood to the park and back, with the image carried, the band, and a priest at the front. It has been done before, years ago, before the parish stopped doing it for reasons nobody wrote down. This year there is a reason people will say aloud: a van has been seen on the avenue, and families have stopped coming to the one o'clock, and a procession with the parish's name on the banner is either a statement that the parish walks with its people in the street or an invitation to have a photograph taken of who was there. {@group_leader} knows both things. He has asked anyway. {@pastor} has said it is a police permit and a liability question and has not said yes or no, which means the vicar at the front of it will be the answer.
events.flavorPrompt: A feast, a band, a van on the avenue. The procession as a public act with two readings, both correct.

choices.label: Walk at the front, in a cope, with the parish banner
choices.outcome: Four hundred people walk and the band plays and the avenue watches. Nobody is stopped. The paper runs a photograph and the caption has the parish's name in it. Two families who had stopped coming are at the one o'clock the next day. A letter arrives at the chancery from a man who lives on the avenue and did not enjoy the band.

choices.label: Process around the parish grounds instead. Keep it off the avenue
choices.outcome: It is a smaller thing in a smaller space and the band is louder for it. {@group_leader} accepts it as the year's compromise and says the avenue will still be there next year. Nobody photographs anything. The families who stopped coming do not come back on account of a procession they could not see.

choices.label: Not this year. Tell him why honestly
choices.outcome: You tell him you are afraid of the van and of what a photograph could cost the people in it, and he says the people in it are already afraid and were asking the parish to be less so. The feast is celebrated in the church. It is beautiful and it stays inside.

events.title: Saturday Afternoons
events.body: The community's requests come through {@group_leader} in a list on Monday: a house blessing, a fifteenth-birthday Mass, a novena that needs a priest on the ninth night, a car, a grandmother in the hospital who wants the sacrament in her own language and will take it in yours if she must. {@pastor} does the ones he can, in the phrases he has learned, and hands the list to you with a look that is half apology. It is four Saturday afternoons. The community does not count them as favors; it counts them as the parish, and a priest who does them is a priest they will bring the next list to, longer. A priest who does not is a priest they will stop asking, which is quieter and worse. The novena is Thursday. The grandmother is today.
events.flavorPrompt: A list on a Monday. The sacramental life of a community as a series of small errands that are not small.

choices.label: Do the list
choices.outcome: The grandmother holds your hand and corrects your pronunciation. The fifteenth birthday has a mariachi and a cake taller than the girl. By the fourth Saturday the list has grown and so has the community's opinion of you. {@group_leader} calls you padre in front of the others.

choices.label: Do the list, and do it in their language
choices.outcome: The grandmother weeps because the words are her words. The novena runs long because you are asked to stay for the food. By the second month {@group_leader} is handing you the list before {@pastor} sees it, and {@pastor} has noticed that too.

choices.label: The grandmother and the novena. The rest can wait for the pastor's Saturdays
choices.outcome: You anoint the grandmother, who corrects your pronunciation, and pray the ninth night of the novena in a living room with the television off. The house and the car wait three weeks. The fifteenth birthday finds a priest at another parish, who is, the family says afterward, very kind. {@group_leader} says nothing about it, which is how you know.

events.title: The Missal in the Sacristy Drawer
events.body: The Latin Mass society at {parish} has its Mass on Sunday afternoons, said by a retired priest who drives in from two counties away and who is, {@group_leader} tells you without drama, dying. The society would like you to learn the older form. They have a missal, a tutor, an altar card set, and the patience of people who have waited before. What they do not have is the bishop's permission for a second celebrant, which under the current norms a parochial vicar must obtain in writing, and which {@bishop} has been granting slowly and, {@group_leader} says, with a face. {@pastor} does not attend the afternoon Mass and does not discuss it. The chancery reads the society's newsletter. A priest who learns the rite is, whatever else he is, a priest the chancery has put on a list, and the list is not a punishment and is not not one. {@group_leader} says the retired priest has perhaps a year. He says it as a question about you.
events.flavorPrompt: A missal, a dying priest, and a permission slip with a bishop's face on it. The rite as something people love, not a faction's flag.

choices.label: Learn it, and write to {@bishop} for permission in your own name
choices.outcome: The tutor is exacting and the Latin comes back faster than you feared. The letter to {@bishop} takes a month to answer and the answer is yes, with conditions and a paragraph about unity you read twice. The society has a priest. The chancery has a name. {@pastor} says only that he hopes you know what you have done, and you think you do.

choices.label: Learn it privately, for when it is needed, and ask no one
choices.outcome: You learn it in the evenings with the tutor and say it once, alone, in the empty church, to see if you can. You do not write to anyone. The society knows and does not say. When the retired priest dies the society asks and you tell them the truth, that you cannot without permission, and the truth is not what they wanted.

choices.label: Tell them you will not, and help them find a priest who will
choices.outcome: You call three retired priests and one religious community and find a man who will drive in on alternate Sundays. It is half a Mass a week and the society knows it. {@group_leader} thanks you formally. The newsletter that month notes that the parish's own clergy were unable to assist, which is accurate and which the chancery reads.

choices.label: Tell them the parish has one rite and the afternoon Mass is not your concern
choices.outcome: {@group_leader} does not argue. The society's newsletter prints your sentence, in quotation marks, above the retired priest's obituary four months later. It is read at the chancery and in the parish across the river and in places you will not learn about for years. The afternoon Mass ends. Some of the society stays for the nine o'clock. Most does not.

events.title: A Courtesy Call
events.body: {@chancellor} calls on a Wednesday, which is unusual, and asks how things are at {parish}, which is more unusual, and then mentions the Latin Mass society's newsletter, which is the point. The newsletter's last issue carried a piece on the bishop's implementation of the current norms that used the word grudging in the second paragraph and your name, warmly, in the fourth. {@chancellor} does not ask whether you wrote it. He asks whether you had seen it before it went out, and whether the society understands that it is a parish group and not an independent publisher, and whether you might, as the priest they seem to listen to, help them understand that. He is pleasant. He says {@bishop} has not seen it, in the tone that means the bishop has. {@group_leader} edits the newsletter and has never once asked you to read a draft, and will take it badly if you ask to.
events.flavorPrompt: A pleasant phone call with a file behind it. The chancery's courtesy as a form of instruction.

choices.label: Tell {@group_leader} the newsletter now crosses your desk before it prints
choices.outcome: He takes it badly and then, because he would rather have a priest than a free hand, agrees. The next issue is milder. {@chancellor} does not call again. The society understands that you are between them and the chancery and are not sure whether that makes you a shield or a wall.

choices.label: Tell {@chancellor} the piece was fair and the society has a right to its opinion
choices.outcome: {@chancellor} says he understands, in a voice that files things. The newsletter continues. Your name appears in it again, and then in a letter from the chancery to {@pastor} that {@pastor} shows you without a word. {@group_leader} would carry you on his shoulders.

choices.label: Tell {@chancellor} the society answers to the pastor, and tell {@pastor} about the call
choices.outcome: {@pastor} says he has never read the newsletter and does not intend to start, and calls {@chancellor} to say so. The call ends. The society, hearing you passed it up, concludes you are not their priest, which was perhaps always true.

events.title: Before the Afternoon Mass
events.body: The Latin Mass society would like confessions heard for an hour before its Sunday afternoon Mass, and would like a priest of the parish to hear them, because the visiting celebrant arrives with fifteen minutes to vest and leaves with the same. {@group_leader} makes the request in a letter, typed, with a copy to {@pastor}, which is how the society does things. The parish's scheduled confessions are Saturday at three. The society's people come to those, some of them, and also do not, because Saturday at three is a line and the society's people prefer a priest who knows what they will confess before they say it. It is an hour on Sunday afternoon between the eleven and dinner. {@pastor} has written on his copy, in pencil, your call.
events.flavorPrompt: A typed letter, a pencil note, and an hour in a confessional. Small, formal, and entirely about belonging.

choices.label: Hear the confessions
choices.outcome: The line is longer than Saturday's. They confess with the precision of people who have prepared, and there is a boy of eleven who has memorized the act of contrition in Latin and says it at speed. {@group_leader} thanks you in the next letter, typed. It is an hour you do not get back and would not trade.

choices.label: Saturday at three is the parish's hour. Tell them so, kindly
choices.outcome: The letter in reply is courteous and short. The society finds a priest from a religious house who comes on alternate Sundays. Its people do not come to Saturday at three. The parish has kept its schedule and lost an hour with a group that keeps count.

events.title: To Be Read at All Masses
events.body: {@bishop}'s pastoral letter arrives with the instruction that it be read at all Masses the following Sunday in place of the homily. It is four pages on the parish as a listening Church: consultation, synodal process, the dignity of the migrant, the poor at the center. It is better written than most. The social justice committee has read it before you have. {@group_leader} has come with a proposal: after the letter, a two-minute announcement from the committee inviting the parish to a listening session in the hall, with a sign-up sheet, and a paragraph the committee has drafted that connects the bishop's words to the county's shelter ordinance vote in three weeks. {@pastor} will read the letter at the Masses he has and has said the announcements are the vicar's. The committee's paragraph is good. It is also the committee's, not the bishop's, and the parish will hear it from a pulpit as one thing.
events.flavorPrompt: A four-page letter and a two-minute paragraph. The pulpit as the place where the bishop's voice and a committee's get confused.

choices.label: Read the letter. Announce the listening session. Cut the paragraph about the vote
choices.outcome: The listening session has forty people and is, by the standard of such things, real. {@group_leader} is disappointed about the paragraph and grateful about the session and says both. The ordinance passes without the parish's paragraph. {@pastor} says you kept the pulpit the bishop's, which he means as praise.

choices.label: Read the letter and the committee's paragraph, vote and all
choices.outcome: The paragraph lands in a church that has not been asked to think about the ordinance and now must. Three people walk out at the nine. Forty come to the session. A letter to the paper, signed by a parishioner, thanks {parish} for its courage, and another, signed by a different parishioner, does not. {@bishop}'s office hears both.

choices.label: Read the letter. No announcement. The bishop said in place of the homily, not in addition
choices.outcome: The letter is read and the parish goes to coffee. {@group_leader} says the bishop asked for a listening Church and the parish's clergy heard him and declined to listen. The session happens anyway, in a member's living room, with eleven people. The committee has decided something about you.

events.title: The Table in the Vestibule
events.body: The social justice committee has a table in the vestibule after the Masses with a petition on it, and {@secretary} has asked you what the parish's policy on petitions is, because the last pastor had one and {@pastor} has not said. The petition is about the county's shelter budget. It is not partisan on its face. {@group_leader} is at the table with a clipboard and a smile that has signed up half the ten o'clock. The pro-life group had a table in the fall with a different clipboard, and nobody asked about policy then, which {@group_leader} will point out if you raise it. It is a table. It is also a thing people will walk past on their way out of Mass and take as the parish's view, or the parish's tolerance of a view, and be right either way.
events.flavorPrompt: A folding table, a clipboard, and a secretary asking about policy. The vestibule as the parish's most political square footage.

choices.label: Let the table stay. A petition is not a candidate
choices.outcome: The table stays for three Sundays and gathers four hundred signatures. Two parishioners write to {@pastor} about it; he forwards them to you. {@group_leader} says the parish has a spine. {@secretary} writes the policy herself and puts your name on it.

choices.label: No petitions in the vestibule from anyone, starting now
choices.outcome: The table comes down. So, in principle, does the pro-life group's, which has not asked for one yet and will. {@group_leader} folds the clipboard with great dignity. {@secretary} is relieved to have a rule. The committee's next meeting is about you.

events.title: The Weekend at the Lake
events.body: The men's group does a weekend retreat every fall at a camp on the lake, thirty men, cabins, a fire, and a speaker. This year's speaker has cancelled and {@group_leader} would like you to lead it. Three talks, a holy hour, confessions Saturday night, Mass Sunday morning, and the thing he actually wants, which is a priest who will sit at the fire until one in the morning and let men who do not talk, talk. He says {@pastor} came once and left after the second talk. The weekend is the same one as the diocesan clergy day, which is optional and attended. The group's retreats have, he says, kept three marriages together that he knows of, and he suspects a fourth. It is a lot of hours. It is the sort of thing a priest is for and the sort of thing that is never on any evaluation.
events.flavorPrompt: A fire, thirty men, and the middle of the night. Masculine reticence without cliché.

choices.label: Lead the retreat and skip the clergy day
choices.outcome: The talks are fine. The fire is the retreat. At half past midnight a man who runs a plumbing company tells you about his brother, and at one a man you have seen at every eight o'clock for a year tells you he has not believed in anything since his daughter died. Sunday Mass at the lake is the best Mass you have said. {@vicar_for_clergy} notes your absence in a tone.
