choices.label: Drive up Saturday afternoon for confessions and Mass. Go to the clergy day Friday
choices.outcome: You hear confessions in a cabin and say Mass on a picnic table and drive home Sunday afternoon. It is a good retreat. It is not the retreat {@group_leader} asked for, and the fire on Saturday night goes on without a priest at it. {@vicar_for_clergy} shakes your hand Friday.

choices.label: Find them a speaker and a chaplain from the religious house. Go to the clergy day
choices.outcome: The friar you find is good and the men like him. He is not theirs. {@group_leader} thanks you for the referral in a way that files it. The group's numbers are steady and its regard for its parish's clergy is what it was, which is to say polite.

events.title: Saturday at Seven
events.body: The men's group meets Saturday mornings at seven in the hall, forty minutes of a video series and forty minutes of eggs, and this month the series has a segment on fatherhood and {@group_leader} would like a priest to speak instead. Twenty minutes. He says the men would like to hear what a celibate makes of fatherhood, which is either the group's idea of a joke or its idea of a serious question, and with this group it is usually both. It is Saturday at seven, the morning you sleep past seven if you sleep past anything. The group has grown this year and is, {@pastor} says with something like suspicion, the one group in the parish whose members show up to help {@maintenance} without being asked.
events.flavorPrompt: Eggs, a video paused on a title card, and a joke that is also a question.

choices.label: Speak for twenty minutes on fatherhood
choices.outcome: You talk about your own father, which you had not planned to, and it is the part they remember. A man in the back asks whether a priest misses having children and you tell him the truth, which is sometimes. The eggs are cold by the time you get to them.

choices.label: Let them run the video. Come for the eggs
choices.outcome: The video is fine and you eat eggs with men who have the good manners not to mention that you were asked to speak and did not. {@group_leader} does not ask again for a while. The group grows anyway, which you notice, and which {@pastor} notices, and which is either a good sign for the group or a bad one for the parish's priests.

events.title: The Eighth Week
events.body: The bereavement group runs in eight-week cycles, and {@group_leader} has designed them carefully: a beginning, an end, a card at the end, a Mass. It works. People come in unable to sit still and leave able to. One woman has been in every cycle for three years. Her husband died in the spring of the first one. She comes early, sets out the chairs, stays late, and has begun, {@group_leader} says, to answer for the others: what they should feel, when they should be done. Two new members left the last cycle in the fourth week. {@group_leader} has asked you, because she cannot, to tell the widow that the group is not hers to keep. She says it the way people say things they have already tried. The widow has your name on the parish's list of people who bring Communion to the homebound, and she is good at it, and it is the only thing she does that is not this.
events.flavorPrompt: Folding chairs set out early. A grief that has become a place to live. No cruelty in the room, only the arithmetic of who else needs the chairs.

choices.label: Ask her to help you start a homebound ministry team. Let her leave the group for something
choices.outcome: She hears it for what it is and also for what you meant, and takes the second. She sets out chairs for a different meeting now. The bereavement group's next cycle keeps all eleven. {@group_leader} says you found the door she could not, and the widow, once, at the sign of peace, holds your hand a second longer.

choices.label: Tell her plainly the group has done what it can for her
choices.outcome: She does not argue and she does not come back, to the group or to the Communion list or to the eight o'clock. You see her once at the pharmacy. The group heals as groups do. {@group_leader} is grateful and cannot look at you for a month.

choices.label: Tell {@group_leader} grief has no schedule, and the widow stays
choices.outcome: {@group_leader} says nothing and finishes the cycle. She does not run the next one. The widow runs it, in effect, and it is a smaller group with a longer memory. Three years later she is still setting out the chairs and the parish has, without deciding to, a group for one person.

events.title: The Names
events.body: The bereavement ministry's Mass of Remembrance is the first week of November: the names of everyone buried from {parish} in the past year read aloud, a candle for each, the families in the front pews, the group in the back with tissues. {@group_leader} runs it and has asked you to preside, because {@pastor} presides at the funerals and she thinks the families should see the other priest at least once with the names. There are sixty-one names this year. Reading them takes eleven minutes and must be done without hurrying and without a wrong pronunciation, and she has provided a sheet with the hard ones spelled out phonetically. The homily should be short. The reception after is the group's, and the families stay for it, and that is where the ministry actually happens.
events.flavorPrompt: Sixty-one names, a phonetic sheet, and the pews where families sit. Plain and exact.

choices.label: Preside, and stay for the reception
choices.outcome: You read sixty-one names without error and the candles go up one at a time. The homily is four minutes. At the reception a man whose wife's name you read tells you he had not been to Mass since the funeral and might come Sunday. {@group_leader} squeezes your arm on the way out.

choices.label: Preside, and leave after the final blessing
choices.outcome: The names are read without error and the candles lit one at a time and you are gone before the coffee is poured. The families notice a little. {@group_leader} notices a lot, and says only that the reception was well attended, and does not say by whom. The man whose wife's name you read leaves before the coffee too.

events.title: The Open Meeting
events.body: The recovery group's anniversary is an open meeting: family, friends, and, this year, a priest to say a few words at the start, which {@group_leader} has asked of you because the group meets in the parish hall and has never once been visited by the parish. You go. There are forty people in a circle of folding chairs and a coffee urn that has seen worse. You say your few words. Then the meeting begins, and the third person to speak, giving a first name and a fact, is the chair of the parish finance council, a man you have sat across from at eleven meetings and who has never, in any of them, said anything that was not about money. He sees you see him. He goes on. He has been sober for four years. The meeting is anonymous by its own tradition and by a discipline older than your ordination. {@group_leader} watches you from across the circle to see what you are going to do with what you now know.
events.flavorPrompt: A circle of chairs, a coffee urn, and a face the player knows from a different table. Anonymity as something sacred and practical at once.

choices.label: Keep it. It was never yours
choices.outcome: You leave when the meeting ends and do not look for him. At the next finance council he passes you the budget and says nothing and you say nothing, and it is the beginning of the only real friendship you have on that council. {@group_leader} nods at you the next time you pass the hall on a Tuesday night.

choices.label: Stay after, and tell {@group_leader} you are not there only as a priest
choices.outcome: She is not surprised, and she does not make anything of it. She gives you the schedule for the closed meetings and tells you there is a priest in the next county who goes to one on Thursdays. You go, once, and then more than once. The finance council chair is there sometimes. Neither of you mentions the parish.

choices.label: Find him in the parking lot and tell him you are glad he is there
choices.outcome: He is not glad you found him. He says, politely, that the whole point is that nobody finds him. He does not come back to the hall's meeting; he drives to one two towns over. He stays on the finance council. {@group_leader} hears about the parking lot and says you meant well, which is what she says about mistakes.

events.title: The Ten O'Clock Meeting
events.body: The recovery group's late meeting ends at ten and the hall is supposed to be locked by nine-thirty, and {@maintenance} has raised it, twice, with {@secretary}, who has raised it with you because {@pastor} said the groups are the vicar's. The late meeting has nine people, all of whom work days. {@group_leader} says a meeting at ten is the difference for two of them between the hall and the bar. {@maintenance} says a hall unlocked at ten is the difference between his evening and his job, and that the coffee is never cleaned up and once there was a cigarette in the stairwell. Both are true. There is a key. There is the question of who holds it and who answers for it. Nobody has proposed cancelling the meeting, which is how you know they are all decent people; they are only tired.
events.flavorPrompt: A key, a coffee urn, and a cigarette in a stairwell. Small logistics carrying a large thing.

choices.label: Give {@group_leader} a key and make her answer for the hall
choices.outcome: She takes the key like a sacrament and signs for it in {@secretary}'s book. The coffee is cleaned up. The cigarette in the stairwell does not recur, or is not found. {@maintenance} says nothing, checks the stairwell every morning for a month, and then stops checking, which is the closest thing he has to trust.

choices.label: Move the meeting to nine and let {@maintenance} lock at nine-thirty
choices.outcome: Seven of the nine can make nine. Two cannot, and one of the two is one of the two. {@group_leader} does not say this to you; she says it to the group. {@maintenance} is grateful and locks up on time for the first time in a year.

events.title: Theology on Tap
events.body: The young adults have booked the back room of a bar downtown for a Thursday night series and would like you to give the first talk: forty minutes on a subject of your choosing, questions, and then the part that is the point, which is a priest at a bar with people his own age until the bar closes. {@group_leader} says {@pastor} came once, years ago, and ordered a club soda and left at nine. The series is a diocesan program with a name and a logo and, she says, the bishop's blessing, in a general way. It is also a photograph of a priest in a bar, which people will take, and a room full of twenty-eight-year-olds, some of whom will be in love with you by the second talk in the way that is not about you. The first one is in ten days. She has already printed the flyer with your name on it.
events.flavorPrompt: A back room, a printed flyer, and a priest young enough to be mistaken for the audience. The pull of being liked.

choices.label: Give the talk and stay until closing
choices.outcome: Sixty people come and forty stay. The questions are better than the talk. You are photographed with a beer and it is fine, mostly. By the third week the group has doubled and {@pastor} has heard, from someone at the deanery, that the vicar at {parish} has a following, which is a word he says to you with care.

choices.label: Give the talk, take questions, and leave at nine with a club soda
choices.outcome: The talk goes well and the questions are good and you are in the car by nine-fifteen. {@group_leader} says it was great in a voice that has already moved on to who might do the next one. The group holds. The photograph nobody takes is the one you were worried about.

choices.label: Tell her you do not do bars, and offer the hall on a Thursday instead
choices.outcome: You do not explain and she does not ask, which is a kindness you notice. The hall on Thursday draws twenty. It is a good twenty. The series in the bar goes on with a Dominican from the university, who is very popular. {@group_leader} does not hold it against you and cannot quite hide that the hall is not the same.

choices.label: Decline. A priest in a bar is a photograph waiting to happen
choices.outcome: She reprints the flyer with a priest from the parish across the river, who is a hit. The group drifts, a little, toward the parish across the river. {@pastor} says you were prudent, in the tone of a man who is not sure prudent was the thing called for.

events.title: Sunday at Seven
events.body: The young adults want a Sunday evening Mass. {@group_leader} has a petition with ninety names, which is more than come to the group, and a plan: seven o'clock, the choir's younger section, a homily they describe as for them, coffee after in the hall. {@pastor} has said the parish has enough Masses and a priest who says five on a weekend does not need six. He has also said that if the vicar wants to add one, the vicar may, and it will be the vicar's. That is a Mass every Sunday evening, permanently, in a church that is otherwise dark by then, for a congregation that will be ninety for a month and forty after. It is also the only hour in the week the group has asked for that is a Mass and not a bar or a hall.
events.flavorPrompt: A petition with ninety names and a pastor's shrug. A Mass as a permanent commitment nobody will thank you for.

choices.label: Add the seven o'clock and make it yours
choices.outcome: Ninety come the first month. Forty come after, and forty is a congregation. The homily is different at seven and you learn to preach it. {@pastor} does not attend and does not object. You have a Mass now, and no Sunday evenings, and a group that has begun to call it ours.

choices.label: Once a month. See whether ninety is ninety
choices.outcome: Once a month, on the first Sunday, sixty come, and it is a good Mass with a real homily and coffee after in the hall. {@group_leader} says monthly is a start, in a voice that means monthly is what she got. The group does not grow and does not shrink. The petition with ninety names goes in her folder, not a drawer.

choices.label: The parish has enough Masses. Tell her so
choices.outcome: She hears it from {@pastor} first and then from you, and the second time is the one that counts, because she had thought you were different. The petition goes in a drawer. The parish across the river has a Sunday at six, and by spring some of the ninety names are in its pews, and she is one of them some weeks.

events.title: Four Chairs
events.body: {@group_leader} has led the group since before you were ordained, and there are four people at its meetings now, and two of them come because she calls them Tuesday afternoon to remind them. She knows. She has told you, in the parking lot after the last one, that she is tired, that her knees are bad, that her daughter wants her to move closer, and that she will not be the one who ends it, because the group was her husband's and he is buried behind the church. She asks you to come next Tuesday. She does not ask you to fix anything. The parish bulletin still lists the group with a meeting time and her phone number. {@pastor} has said, when asked, that groups end when they end and it is not the clergy's job to bury them. He has also said that she is a saint and that he will not be the one to tell her.
events.flavorPrompt: Four chairs and a leader who cannot put down what she is carrying. Tenderness without softness.

choices.label: Go Tuesday and keep going, and let it be four chairs with a priest in one
choices.outcome: You go for a year. It is four chairs and then three. She talks about her husband and you learn the parish from her. When she moves to her daughter's the group ends with a card and a Mass, and the card is signed by three people and a priest. It was not nothing. It was an hour a week, for a year.

choices.label: Offer to end it with her: a final meeting, a Mass for her husband, a line in the bulletin
choices.outcome: She says no and then, a week later, calls to say yes. The final meeting has fourteen people, which is more than it has had in years, because you announced it. The Mass is for her husband. The bulletin line is one sentence. She weeps in the sacristy and thanks you, and means it, and does not come to the eight o'clock for a month.

choices.label: Find her a successor and tell her the group is safe to hand over
choices.outcome: You ask three people and the third says yes, a younger woman with the energy for calls on Tuesday afternoons. {@group_leader} hands over the phone list like a key and is, for a month, bereft, and then relieved. The group is not what it was. It is something.

choices.label: Leave it in the bulletin. It is hers
choices.outcome: It is hers and it goes on being hers until it is two chairs, and then she does not call the second one. The bulletin lists it for another year. {@secretary} takes it out eventually without asking anyone. Nobody notices, which was the thing she was afraid of.

events.title: The Standing Committee
events.body: The group has five members, a bank account, a line in the bulletin, a closet in the hall with its name on the door, and {@group_leader}, who has been its president for eleven years and who describes it, at parish council, as one of the parish's most active ministries. The council knows. {@pastor} knows. Nobody has said it, because {@group_leader} is on the council and the finance council and the liturgy committee and knows where everything is. This month a newer parishioner asked at council whether the closet might be shared with the youth group, which has sixty kids and no closet. {@group_leader} said the group's materials were in it. The materials are three banners and a coffee urn. She has asked you, as the priest who attends council, to speak to the newer parishioner about respect for the parish's established ministries. The youth group has asked you about the closet.
events.flavorPrompt: A closet with a name on the door. Institutional life at its most granular. The leader is not a villain; she is a person with a closet.

choices.label: Give the youth group the closet and tell her the group keeps its line in the bulletin
choices.outcome: She takes it as the beginning of the end, which it is, and says so to everyone at coffee for a month. The youth group has a closet. The five members meet twice more and then do not. {@group_leader} remains on three committees and remembers this.

choices.label: Propose folding the group into something living, with her as honorary chair
choices.outcome: You write a paragraph for council in which the group becomes a committee of a larger ministry and {@group_leader} its founding chair in perpetuity. She reads it three times and accepts. The closet is shared. The banners hang at the ministry fair. It is a fiction and it is a kind one and everyone at council knows which.

choices.label: Speak to the newer parishioner about respect. It costs nothing
choices.outcome: It costs something. The newer parishioner stops coming to council and, in time, to {parish}. The youth group keeps its supplies in a van. {@group_leader} thanks you and adds you to the list of people she can count on, which is a list that has uses.

events.title: Everyone Loves Her
events.body: The group is the best thing in the parish and everyone says so, and everyone also says, a sentence later and more quietly, that it is {@group_leader}'s. She founded it, or refounded it, or was there so early nobody remembers the difference. Its members are devoted. Its former members are a longer list, and this month one of them, a woman you have anointed twice in the hospital, tells you why she left: the meeting where {@group_leader} read aloud, to the whole group, a private note the woman had written her, and asked whether anyone else felt that way. Nobody did. Two others have told you versions. None of them will say it in a room with {@group_leader} in it, because she is very good, and the group is very good, and the parish would defend her against a bishop. {@pastor} has heard the stories for years and has said that the group does more good than the stories do harm. That may be true. You are the priest the former members are talking to.
events.flavorPrompt: A leader who is genuinely excellent and genuinely cruel, and a parish that has decided which one to see. The dilemma should feel unfair in every direction.

choices.label: Sit down with her privately and tell her what you have heard
choices.outcome: She listens with the face of someone who has heard it before and has an answer for each name. Her answers are good. Then she asks whether you are questioning her leadership, and you say you are questioning one meeting, and she says she will pray about it, which is a way of ending the conversation. The group's next meeting is warm. You are not mentioned at it, which is how you know you were.

choices.label: Ask the former members to put it in writing, for {@pastor}
choices.outcome: Two of the three write it down. {@pastor} reads the letters and puts them in a drawer with the others, and says that now there is a file, and that files are how things end. He does not say when. {@group_leader} learns there is a file. The group has never been more devoted to her.

choices.label: The group does more good than the stories do harm. Let it lie
choices.outcome: You tell the woman you anointed that you are sorry and that the group is not the parish, and she says she knows, and does not come back to either. The group thrives. {@group_leader} hears you were approached and did nothing and is warmer to you after, which you notice and do not enjoy.

events.title: The Meeting After the Meeting
events.body: It happens in public this time. At the group's spring meeting {@group_leader} stands and names a member, a nineteen-year-old who missed three weeks for a hospitalized mother, and says the group has no room for people who are not committed, and the nineteen-year-old leaves in front of forty people. Three of them follow her out. By Monday the story has reached {@pastor} from four directions, and he has done what he does, which is to ask you into his office and close the door and say that something has to happen now and that the something will be done by the priest the group's people talk to. He does not say what. He says the group is the best thing in the parish. He says {@group_leader} has given it eleven years. He says the nineteen-year-old's mother is a parishioner and is dying. He says he will back whatever you decide, in the tone of a man who has decided to be backed. The group meets Thursday.
events.flavorPrompt: A closed door and a pastor delegating the knife. The leader has finally done the thing in front of witnesses, which changes everything and nothing.

choices.label: Ask for her resignation Thursday, in front of the group, and name a successor
choices.outcome: She does not resign; she is removed, and she says so to everyone. Half the group leaves with her and meets in her living room. The other half stays and is, within a year, a group again, smaller and kinder. The parish is divided about you for a long time. The nineteen-year-old comes back. Her mother dies in June and {@group_leader} does not come to the funeral.

choices.label: Meet her privately with the file and offer her a graceful exit before Thursday
choices.outcome: You put the letters on the table and let her read them. She reads them all. She says she will announce Thursday that she is stepping down for her health, and you say the parish will thank her from the pulpit, and it does. The group wobbles and holds. The nineteen-year-old comes back. {@group_leader} sits in the back pew now and does not speak to you, and the parish never knows why.

choices.label: Reprimand her Thursday, restore the nineteen-year-old, and keep her as leader
choices.outcome: You say, in front of forty people, that the group has room for anyone whose mother is dying, and that the nineteen-year-old is welcome, and {@group_leader} says of course, of course, in a voice that will not forgive you. The nineteen-year-old comes back for two meetings. The group thrives. It is hers. Nothing has changed except that everyone now knows a priest watched it happen and chose the group.

choices.label: Tell {@pastor} it is his group, his parish, and his decision, and you will support it
choices.outcome: He is quiet for a long moment and then says that he had hoped for better. He does nothing. The nineteen-year-old does not come back. Her mother's funeral is in June and {@group_leader} runs the luncheon. The group is the best thing in the parish. You are a man who was asked and said it was not his.

effects.key: Declined to act on a lay leader's public cruelty when asked

events.title: Three Weeks In
events.body: {@group_leader} took over the group three weeks ago because the previous leader moved and nobody else would, and has come to your office with a legal pad and a list of questions that begins with how do I reserve the hall and ends with what do I do about the two people who have hated each other since before I joined. The group is larger than anyone told her. It has a bank account she has not been given the password to. It has a tradition of a spring dinner that requires forty volunteers and a liquor license. She is competent and frightened and has taken a day off work to sit in your office, and she is asking, without saying it, whether you are going to be the priest who helps her or the priest who signs things. {@pastor} has said that lay leaders should lead and clergy should stay out of it, which is a principle and also a way of not being in the room.
events.flavorPrompt: A legal pad, a bank account with no password, and a new leader who has not yet learned that nobody will help her unless someone decides to. Practical and kind.

choices.label: Give her an hour a week for two months
choices.outcome: You go through the pad. You get her the password, walk her through the hall calendar, and, the fourth week, sit with her and the two people who hate each other while they do not resolve anything and agree to stop doing it at meetings. By spring she does not need the hour and keeps coming anyway, with coffee, to tell you what is happening.

choices.label: Answer the pad today and send her to {@secretary} for the rest
choices.outcome: You answer everything on the pad in forty minutes. {@secretary} gets her the password and the calendar. The two people who hate each other are still there. The spring dinner happens, somehow. She has learned that the parish has a system and that the priest is not part of it.

choices.label: Lay leaders lead. Tell her, gently, that it is her group
choices.outcome: She thanks you and leaves with the pad. The spring dinner does not happen. The two people who hate each other are joined by a third. In the fall she asks {@pastor} whether someone else might take over, and he tells her lay leaders lead, and she does, until she does not.

events.title: The Thing You Started
events.body: The group you founded is failing, and it is failing in the way things fail in parishes, which is that nobody stops coming all at once. Attendance is half what it was in the spring. {@group_leader}, whom you recruited, has begun to send the meeting reminders on the morning of, which is a thing people do when they are hoping nobody comes. The room you fought {@secretary} for is booked by someone else on the nights you skip. You know exactly what happened: you gave it a year of evenings and then the parish gave you other evenings, and the group was built on you in a way you did not intend and could not have avoided. {@pastor} has not mentioned it, which is his kindness. The bulletin still lists it. Two of the remaining members have asked you, separately and carefully, whether you are still interested. It is the question that ends groups and the question that saves them.
events.flavorPrompt: A founder watching his founding thin out. No self-pity; the failure is ordinary and structural and his.

choices.label: Give it the evenings again, for a season
choices.outcome: You are there every week for three months and the room fills back up, because it was always you they came for. {@group_leader} is grateful and knows what it means, which is that it will happen again. You have bought a season. You have not built anything that stands without you, and you know it now in a way you did not before.

choices.label: Step back on purpose. Put {@group_leader} in front and stay out of the room
choices.outcome: You tell her it is hers, and mean it, and then you do the harder thing, which is not to come. It shrinks further. Then it stops shrinking. Six months later it is smaller than it was and it is not yours, and {@group_leader} runs it with a voice that has stopped checking the door for you. It will survive your transfer. That was the point.

choices.label: Let it end. Not everything you start has to last
choices.outcome: You tell the two members the truth and the group has one more meeting, which is a good one. {@group_leader} is relieved and sad in the proportion that shows she was right to be both. The bulletin line comes out. {@pastor} says he has buried more of his own than you have, in a tone that is not unkind.

events.title: Bigger Than the Room
events.body: The group you founded is the parish's success story and has become, this year, the deanery's. {@group_leader} has been asked to speak about it at a diocesan gathering. Two other parishes have asked for the model, which is a word that now attaches to the thing you started in a borrowed room with nine people. The group has a logo. It has a leadership team, none of whom you recruited. It has scheduled its fall retreat without asking whether you are free, and when you mentioned it, {@group_leader} said, with real warmth, that they did not want to burden you. She meant it. The group does not need you, which is what you built it to do, and there is a feeling that comes with that which you had not been warned about. {@pastor} has noticed the diocesan invitation and has said, in the tone of a man who has watched younger priests before, that it is a fine thing to have founded something and a finer thing to have let it go.
events.flavorPrompt: Success as a small bereavement. The founder learns what it means to have built something that stands. Clear-eyed; no bitterness.

choices.label: Let it go. Go to the retreat as a guest if invited, and not otherwise
choices.outcome: You are invited, as a guest, and you go, and you sit in the back. {@group_leader} thanks you from the front in a sentence that makes you sound like history. The parish across the river starts a chapter. You have founded something. It has a life. You have your evenings and an unfamiliar quiet.

choices.label: Ask to give the talk at the diocesan gathering yourself. It was your idea
choices.outcome: {@group_leader} says of course, and gives up the slot, and the gathering hears about the model from its founder. It goes well. The chancery remembers your name. The leadership team has a meeting afterward that you are not at, about what the group is, and the answer is a little less than it was. {@pastor} says nothing, at length.

choices.label: Ask {@group_leader} to name you chaplain, so the group has a priest as it grows
choices.outcome: She agrees at once, because it costs her nothing, and you have a title and a seat at the leadership team's meetings and a reason to go to the retreat. It is a good arrangement. It is also a way of staying, and the group knows it, and is kind about it.

events.title: Copied to the Bishop
events.body: {@vicar_for_clergy} calls on a Monday to say that the chancery has received a letter, four pages, from {@group_leader}, on the group's letterhead, copied to {@bishop}, concerning the parochial vicar of {parish}. He reads you the subject line and not the letter. It concerns, he says, your treatment of the group, your public remarks, your unavailability, and an incident he describes as the thing with the hall. He says {@bishop} has not read it and will. He says letters like this arrive weekly and mean nothing and go in a file, and that the file is read when assignments are made. He asks whether {@pastor} knows about it. {@pastor} does not. He asks whether you would like to respond in writing, and adds that most priests who respond in writing wish they had not. {@group_leader} is at the eight o'clock the next morning, in the third pew, and receives Communion from your hand.
events.flavorPrompt: A phone call, a subject line, and a Communion line. The chancery's neutrality as its own kind of pressure.

choices.label: Go to {@group_leader} that week, without the letter, and ask what it would take
choices.outcome: It takes two hours at her kitchen table and an apology for the thing with the hall that you had not thought you owed. She does not withdraw the letter. She writes a second one, shorter, saying the matter is resolved. {@vicar_for_clergy} staples them together. The group is not yours, and it is no longer against you.

choices.label: Respond in writing, point by point
choices.outcome: Your letter is accurate, well organized, and six pages. {@vicar_for_clergy} reads it and calls to say it is a very complete letter. It goes in the file beside hers, where it makes you look like a man who writes six pages about a hall. {@group_leader} hears that you replied and writes again.

choices.label: Tell {@pastor} and let him call {@vicar_for_clergy} himself
choices.outcome: {@pastor} is angry to learn of it second and makes the call anyway, and says what pastors say, which is that his vicar is a good priest and the woman is a difficult woman. It helps. It also makes you a priest whose pastor had to call. {@group_leader} takes the group's next event to the parish across the river.

choices.label: Say nothing. Let the file be the file
choices.outcome: You say nothing, to anyone. The letter sits in the file and the group sits in the third pew and you give her Communion every morning, and the file is opened, one day, by a man deciding where to send you, and the letter is four pages and there is nothing beside it.

events.title: Thursday Nights
events.body: The hall is booked twice on Thursday nights and has been since September, and the two bookings have been resolving it by arriving early. {@group_leader}'s group has the calendar entry. {@parishioner}, who runs the other group, has a verbal agreement with the previous secretary, who is dead. This Thursday the two groups set up at opposite ends of the hall and held their meetings simultaneously, and one of them used the microphone. {@secretary} has brought it to you with the calendar open and the face of someone who would like a decision from a priest so that the decision is not hers. {@pastor} has said the hall is a scheduling matter. It is a scheduling matter in the way a will is a paperwork matter. There is one hall. There is a school gym that smells of floor wax and is available. There is the church basement, which floods. Whoever gets Thursday gets the parish's best room and the other gets to remember who gave it away.
events.flavorPrompt: Two folding-table encampments in one hall. Comic on the surface, permanent underneath.

choices.label: The calendar entry stands. {@parishioner}'s group takes the gym
choices.outcome: {@group_leader} is gracious in the manner of a winner. {@parishioner}'s group moves to the gym and loses a quarter of its people to the smell of floor wax. {@parishioner} tells the story at every coffee for a year, and the story has your name in it.

choices.label: Alternate weeks. Both groups take the gym half the time
choices.outcome: Nobody is happy and nobody is wronged, and both groups lose a few people to the alternation, and {@secretary} keeps a color-coded calendar that becomes, over time, the parish's real constitution. {@group_leader} and {@parishioner} nod at each other in the parking lot.

choices.label: Get the basement fixed so there are two rooms. Ask {@pastor} for the money
choices.outcome: It costs four thousand dollars and a plumber who owes {@maintenance} a favor. The basement is dry by Advent. Both groups keep Thursday. {@pastor} says you have solved a problem by spending money he did not have, which is, he says, how pastors solve problems, and he says it almost warmly.

events.title: Above the Fold
events.body: The bulletin has one front page and this week two groups want it. {@group_leader} has a fundraiser Sunday and submitted first. {@parishioner}, whose group has a speaker the same weekend, submitted second and then called {@pastor} at home, which is a thing people do once. {@pastor} has told {@secretary} that the vicar handles the bulletin now, a sentence that was not true until he said it. {@secretary} has the layout open. The front page holds one box. The inside pages hold everything else and are read by the people who read everything, who are the same forty people every week. Whoever is inside will say they were buried. Whoever is on the front will say nothing, which is the only kind of gratitude the bulletin generates. It goes to the printer at noon.
events.flavorPrompt: A layout screen and a noon deadline. The bulletin as the parish's only front page.

choices.label: First submitted, front page. Tell {@parishioner} so
choices.outcome: {@group_leader}'s box runs on the front page and the fundraiser has its best Sunday in years. {@parishioner} says buried, as predicted, and adds that some people call the pastor at home for a reason. {@secretary} writes down the rule you just made so that it will exist next time, and it does, and it has your name on it.

choices.label: Split the box. Half each, smaller type
choices.outcome: Both groups are on the front and neither can be read without glasses. {@secretary} says the box was not designed to be halved and that the printer has opinions about type sizes. Both leaders thank you in a way that suggests they will remember it as a loss, and both events are, in the end, adequately attended.

choices.label: Give {@parishioner} the pulpit announcement and {@group_leader} the front page
choices.outcome: You announce the speaker from the ambo at every Mass and the fundraiser runs on the front. Both are heard. {@pastor} says the announcements ran long. It is a good week for the bulletin and a long one for the Mass.

events.title: Chaplain
events.body: {@group_leader} has asked, formally, in a letter with the group's name at the top, whether you would serve as the group's chaplain. It is a real office in the group's bylaws and it has been vacant since a priest who is now a monsignor somewhere else held it. It means Mass for the group monthly, a talk at each meeting, attendance at the board, a blessing at every event, and the standing expectation, unwritten, that you will be the priest who answers the phone. {@pastor} was asked years ago and declined, and the group has not forgiven him for it, and has noticed that you are not him. The title is nothing. The hours are two or three a week, forever, or until you are moved, at which point the group will feel it as a bereavement and say so to the chancery. {@group_leader} has left the letter on your desk with a pen beside it, which is either a joke or not.
events.flavorPrompt: A letter with a pen beside it. The office as a permanent claim on the week, offered with love.

choices.label: Accept. Sign the letter
choices.outcome: You are chaplain. The board meets on the first Tuesday and you are at it, and the phone rings when it rings. The group is the most loyal thing in your life at {parish}. Your Tuesdays are gone. {@pastor} says the group has captured you, which is his word for it and also true.

choices.label: Accept the Mass and the blessings. Decline the board
choices.outcome: You write back with a paragraph that says yes to the sacramental and no to the structural, and {@group_leader} reads it twice and accepts it, because half a chaplain is more than the group has had. The phone still rings. You answer it less. It is an arrangement that works until it is tested.

choices.label: Decline, as {@pastor} did, and say why
choices.outcome: You say a vicar is assigned to a parish and not to a group, and that you will be the group's priest as you are everyone's. {@group_leader} takes the letter back and the pen. The group's bylaws keep the office vacant. It is not forgiven; it is understood, which is colder.

events.title: Line Item
events.body: The group has asked the parish for three thousand dollars. {@group_leader} has put it in writing, which is more than most groups do: a conference in the spring, a bus, registrations for eleven people, and a paragraph on how it will renew the group's leadership, which it might. {@pastor} has sent the request to you with a note that says what do you think, which means he does not want to say no himself. The parish's discretionary budget for groups is four thousand dollars for the year and it is October. The group has never asked before. It has also never accounted for the money it raises, and {@group_leader}'s treasurer is her husband. Three thousand dollars is a month of the boiler fund or a fifth of the assessment shortfall or, in {@group_leader}'s paragraph, the future of the group. She has asked to hear by Friday because the registration deadline is Monday.
events.flavorPrompt: A request in writing and a budget that was never big enough. Dull and consequential. Nobody is dishonest and nobody is transparent.

choices.label: Fund it in full. Recommend yes
choices.outcome: {@pastor} signs the check with an expression. Eleven people go and come back louder. The group has a year it will talk about for a decade. The three other groups that hear about it ask in November, and the budget is a thousand dollars, and you are the priest who said yes to the first one.

choices.label: Fund half, on condition the group opens its books to the finance council
choices.outcome: You write two paragraphs about accountability that {@group_leader} reads as an accusation and then, because the money is real, accepts. The books turn out to be fine, kept by the husband in a spreadsheet nobody had asked to see. Six people go. The finance council learns that groups have money, which is a thing it will now want to discuss.

choices.label: Offer a match: the parish gives what the group raises, up to fifteen hundred
choices.outcome: The group raises eleven hundred in three weeks, which is more than it has raised in three years, and the parish gives eleven hundred, and eight people go. {@group_leader} is annoyed at the arithmetic and pleased with the group. {@pastor} thinks it was clever, which he says as a warning.

choices.label: Recommend no. The boiler is the boiler
choices.outcome: {@pastor} writes the no on your recommendation and says so in the letter. {@group_leader} does not go to the conference and does not forget who was asked and what he thought. The boiler fund is three thousand dollars closer to a boiler, which nobody thanks you for either.

events.title: Carrying Her
events.body: {@group_leader} lost her husband in the winter and has not missed a meeting, and the group has been carrying her since, which it is glad to do and has begun to say so, which is the sign that it is tired. She arrives with agendas she does not follow. She weeps at announcements. The meeting last week ran ninety minutes over because she could not stop talking about the funeral, which the group attended and organized and paid for. Two members have come to you: they love her, they want her to stay, and they want the group back. They have asked you to talk to her. They have asked you not to say they asked. {@pastor} buried the husband and has said he will not add to her grief with a conversation about agendas, which is right and which leaves the conversation to you. She is at daily Mass every morning in the front pew and holds your hand at the sign of peace a second longer than the rite requires.
events.flavorPrompt: A widow leading a meeting she cannot lead and a group that loves her and is exhausted. The tenderness has to be real and so does the exhaustion.

choices.label: Visit her weekly for a season. Let the group's business wait
choices.outcome: You sit in her kitchen on Wednesday afternoons and she talks about him. It takes three months for the meetings to shorten and six for her to run one. The two members who came to you carry it in the meantime and do not say they asked. The group has a leader again, eventually, and it is her.

choices.label: Propose a co-leader for a year, in her hearing, as a kindness
choices.outcome: You say it at the end of a meeting, gently, as if it were about the group's growth, and she says yes before the sentence is finished, because she has been waiting for someone to let her. The co-leader runs the meetings. She attends them. The group breathes. She knows what you did and thanks you for it a year later.

choices.label: Tell her the group needs her to step back for a season
choices.outcome: She hears it as the group sending a priest to fire her, which is what it is. She steps back. She stops coming to daily Mass for a month and then comes back to the side aisle. The group recovers. Something between you and her does not, and the two members who asked never say so.

choices.label: Grief takes what it takes. Tell the two members so
choices.outcome: They nod and keep carrying her. By summer they are not at the meetings either. The group has four people and a widow with an agenda she does not follow. {@pastor} says you were right not to add to her grief, and you were, and there is now no group.

events.title: The Mailing List
events.body: {@group_leader} is running for the school board. The announcement was on the group's social page before it was anywhere else, and the group's mailing list, which is a hundred and eighty parish families, received a message the same day that did not mention the election and did mention the candidate's long service to {parish}. Two parishioners have forwarded it to {@pastor} with the word appropriate and a question mark. {@pastor} has forwarded it to you with no words. The group is good. {@group_leader} built it. The mailing list was assembled from the parish's own database, which {@secretary} exported for the group two years ago because nobody had thought about it. The school board race is nonpartisan on paper and not otherwise. The parish's tax status is a sentence in a diocesan policy that {@chancellor} can recite. {@group_leader} would say, and has, that the message was about the group.
events.flavorPrompt: A social page, an exported database, and a candidate who is also a good lay leader. The line between service and campaign, drawn in a parish that does not want to draw it.

choices.label: Take the mailing list back to the parish. Nothing goes out without {@secretary}
choices.outcome: {@group_leader} calls it a seizure and says so to the group. The list goes back to the office. The next message to a hundred and eighty families comes from {@secretary} and is about a bake sale. {@group_leader} wins the seat. The group continues under a leader who now sits on a public body and remembers.

choices.label: A quiet word: keep the campaign and the group apart, and no one has to say anything
choices.outcome: She hears it, because it is you. The group's page goes quiet on the election. The mailing list is used for the group. She wins, and the parish does not appear in the story of how. {@pastor} never learns what you said and does not ask, which is his gift.

choices.label: It is a school board. Leave it
choices.outcome: Three more messages go out before the election, and the third is about the election. A parishioner who lost the race writes to {@chancellor}. {@chancellor} calls {@pastor}. {@pastor} says he sent it to the vicar. The group wins a seat on the school board and the parish gets a letter in a file.

events.title: No One After Her
events.body: {@group_leader} is the reason the group works. Everyone says it, and unlike most things everyone says, it is true: she calls the sick, she remembers the birthdays, she is at the hall at six to set up and at nine to sweep, and she has never once, in anyone's hearing, said a word about herself. This month she told you, after the eight o'clock, that she has a diagnosis. She said it as one says the weather. She has not told the group. She has, she says, perhaps a year of being useful. She asked you not to say anything, and to think about who comes after her, because she has thought about it and there is no one. The group has forty members and none of them has ever had to do anything, because she did it. She asks you to think about it and then she goes to sweep the hall. {@pastor} does not know. She would prefer he did not.
events.flavorPrompt: A saint with a diagnosis, said like the weather. The prose should not sentimentalize her and should not underrate what she is.

choices.label: Quietly build a leadership team around her this year, with her help
choices.outcome: She helps. She hands over the birthday list first, and then the sick list, and then the key, each to a different person, each with a reason that is not the real one. By the time she tells the group there are five people doing what she did, badly, and she says that is fine. The group survives her. It is never as good, and it knows why.

choices.label: Walk with her through the year. Let the group be what it is until it is not
choices.outcome: You visit her every week and anoint her twice and say the funeral, which the group organizes and does well, because she left a list. The group meets for a year afterward and then does not, because there was never a second person. The parish remembers her name. The bulletin has a blank where the group was.

choices.label: Tell {@pastor}. He should know what the parish is about to lose
choices.outcome: He knows what to do with it, which is to visit her, and he does, and she knows you told him and does not mention it. He names a successor from the parish council over her head. The successor is competent. The group is a committee by the following spring, and she attends it, in the back, until she cannot.

events.title: Everyone Wants Thursday
events.body: It is Holy Week and every group in {parish} has sent a request, and {@group_leader}'s is the one on top: the group would like to lead the watch at the altar of repose on Thursday night until midnight, with the group's own prayers, and would like you present for the whole of it. Beneath it are the others: the choir's rehearsal that needs a priest to walk the Exsultet, the youth group's Stations on Friday afternoon, the ethnic community's procession, the Knights' honor guard, the guild's linens. {@pastor} has the Chrism Mass Thursday morning and the liturgies themselves and has said the vicar takes the groups. There are more hours asked than there are hours. You will fail someone this week; that is what the week is. The question is who, and whether you tell them beforehand or let them find out by your absence. {@group_leader}'s letter ends with the sentence that the group has kept the watch for thirty years and would not know how to keep it without a priest.
events.flavorPrompt: The week that breaks every year. A stack of letters and a body with one set of hours. No heroics; triage.

choices.label: Keep the watch with {@group_leader}'s group until midnight. Let the others find deacons
choices.outcome: You kneel at the altar of repose from the end of the Mass until midnight, and the group's prayers are old and long, and you do not remember the last hour. The youth Stations are led by {@dre}. The choir walks the Exsultet without you and it shows Saturday night. {@group_leader} says the group will remember it. Friday morning you cannot stand up straight.

choices.label: An hour at the watch, an hour at rehearsal, the Stations. Tell everyone beforehand
choices.outcome: You write four notes Tuesday and keep all four promises, badly. The watch has you until nine. The Exsultet is walked. The Stations are led. Nobody got the whole of you and everyone got the note, which they mention, with something between gratitude and grievance. {@group_leader}'s note is the one she keeps.

choices.label: The liturgies and nothing else. Every group finds its own way this year
choices.outcome: You are at every liturgy and nowhere else, and you are rested for the Vigil, and the Vigil is the best you have sung it. The watch is kept by the group without a priest for the first time in thirty years. {@group_leader}'s letter the following week is one paragraph and is about the group's disappointment, and it is copied to {@pastor}.

events.title: Let It Die
events.body: {@pastor} says it over dinner, not looking up: the group is finished, he has decided, and he would like you to see to it. Not a letter, not an announcement. He would like the hall bookings to lapse, the bulletin line to disappear, the requests for a priest to go unanswered until the group understands. He says {@group_leader} will call the chancery and the chancery will do nothing, because the chancery has heard from her before. He says it is his parish and he is not asking. He gives reasons: the group's numbers, its tone, a thing {@group_leader} said to him in the sacristy at Easter that he does not repeat. Some of the reasons are good. The group has twelve people who have been faithful to it for years and who will feel this as a wound they cannot name, because nobody will have said anything. You have been asked to do a quiet thing quietly, by the man whose parish it is, and you are a vicar.
events.flavorPrompt: An order given over dinner without eye contact. Obedience as a real thing with a real cost. The pastor is not a monster and the order is not clean.

choices.label: Do as he asks. Let the bookings lapse
choices.outcome: It takes four months. The group meets in a member's home for a while and then does not. {@group_leader} calls the chancery, which does nothing, and calls you, which you do not return, and it is the not returning you remember. {@pastor} thanks you once, briefly, and never mentions it again.

choices.label: Do it, but tell {@group_leader} to her face that it is ending and why
choices.outcome: {@pastor} did not want it said aloud and you say it aloud, in her kitchen, with the reasons you can give. She calls the chancery and the chancery does nothing. She calls you and you answer. The group ends with a Mass she asks you to say. {@pastor} says you were not asked to be honest, and you say you were not asked not to be.

choices.label: Tell him you will not be the instrument of a thing he will not say himself
choices.outcome: He looks up. He says a vicar who chooses which orders to follow is not a vicar. He does it himself, in writing, and the letter is colder than yours would have been. {@group_leader} blames him and not you, which is correct and does not help. It is a long year in the rectory.

choices.label: Ask for six months to turn it around before he ends it
choices.outcome: He gives you six months because you asked and because it is easier than arguing. You give the group an evening a week and a new project and a conversation with {@group_leader} about the sacristy at Easter. At six months it has twenty people and a tone. {@pastor} does not end it, and does not say he was wrong, and it is enough.
